item.title: What is Entropy ? — Intuitive explanation with code.
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
You may be familiar with variance, it is a useful measure when looking for how spread the data is. When I say spread, I'm referring to the dispersion of data around the sample's mean. Indeed, when the data is very spread it is often considered that it contains a lot of information. I say often because sometimes the data can be spread but it is not information, only noise. The concept of information is very important in Statistics and thus in Data Science. Entropy is one of those concepts that sounds magical at first and that is easily misunderstood and poorly taught. I'll try to keep this article as simple as possible, without using anything from information theory.

Consider those two examples:

A = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
B = [0, 1, 1, 2, 2]

In the list A there’s barely any information because the value is always the same, you won’t learn anything from there. In contrast, the list B contains several different values, which means you’ll probably learn something from it if those values are relevant. This concept might ring you a bell.

The concept of Entropy or Shannon Entropy has some similarities with variance. It is also a way to quantify the amount of information in the data. However, it is somewhat different than variance in the sense that it actually doesn’t care about the values themselves. Entropy is only interested in their probabilities. Let's stick with this idea of using probabilities to describe a system. Notice that in list A the probability associated with 0 is 100% but at the same time we said that there's no information. In this regard, we can say that the more uncertainty there is, the more information there is.

Let's put words on the previous lists and let say you want to choose a country for your summer holidays. You want to choose the country so that you maximize the probability that the wether is sunny. The following lists contain the forecasts for the 5 coming days.

A = [Sunny, Sunny, Sunny, Sunny, Sunny]
B = [Sunny, Cloudy, Cloudy, Rainy, Rainy]

Now it becomes clear that you'll choose country A as country B has an uncertain weather (a high entropy)

In this case, it's not very informative, thus it has low entropy.

In the second case, there is more variety (more information or higher entropy), the probabilities are spread across sunny, cloudy and rainy. With variety comes a way more complete information.

To put it in a nutshell, entropy is a way of quantifying uncertainty. This is probably the most intuitive way to see it. Uncertainty is inversely proportional to probability, that is to say, the more uncertain an outcome is, the least probable it is. As you might have guessed, the uncertainty is maximum when the distribution is uniform (all the probabilities are the same), basically it's a stalemate, it's chaos, you can't take any decision based on the probabilities... which is exactly the scenario where we said that information is maximum. Maximizing information is equivalent to maximizing uncertainty.

Intuition behind the formula

That's pretty much it, entropy is used to describe a probability distribution. Now, I don't want to give you the formula yet, instead I would like to try to re-build it from scratch.

Imagine that you are given a bunch of different distributions and you have to find the one that has the least information/uncertainty. That is to say that the dream scenario would be to have one bar with 100% and 0% probability for all the others. The worst scenario would be to have all the probabilities equally distributed (note that what we do here is basically what's done in decision trees where we try to minimize uncertainty or impurity).

Now, with which formula/metric would you come up with to characterize theses states ?

The first thing I would try in this situation is to multiply all the probabilities together. The reasoning behind it is, as all the probabilities should add up to 1, one would expect that if a probability is very high, the others would be very low, thus all the tiny probabilities will make the whole product shrink to something near zero.

In contrast if the probabilities are all equally distributed, it prevents from having a very tiny probability that will make our product close to zero.

for instance:
A = [98%, 1%, 1%]--> 0.98 * 0.01 * 0.01 = 0.000098

B = [33%, 33%, 33%]--> 0.33 * 0.33 * 0.33 = 0.037

Note that I didn't want to take the scénario [100%, 0%, 0%] as it's obvious that any zero in the list would lead to a product of 0.

It looks like it's working ! B has the highest information/uncertainty. However it's quite annoying to deal with very small numbers (look at A). Multiplying many numbers smaller than 1 leads to very tiny results. A cool way to address this is to use the logarithm function because the product becomes a sum:
log(a*b) = log(a) + log(b)

Also, log is a monotonically increasing function, thus it doesn't change the relations of order.

A --> log(0.98 * 0.01 * 0.01) = log(0.98) + log(0.01) + log(0.01) = - 9.23

B --> log(0.33 * 0.33 * 0.33) = log(0.33) + log(0.33) + log(0.33) = -3.29

B remains the one that has the highest uncertainty and the numbers are not tiny ! But guess what, there's another issue. Indeed log(x) tends to -infinity when x approaches 0.

A trick to address this is to multiply log(p) by p because x*log(x) tends towards 0 when x approaches 0.

A --> 0.98*log(0.98) + 0.01*log(0.01) + 0.01*log(0.01) = - 0.11

B --> 0.33*log(0.33) + 0.33*log(0.33) + 0.33*log(0.33) = -1.09

This time the relation of order is changed (I'll explain why later), and a way to address this issue is to multiply the whole thing by -1.

A --> -1* [0.98*log(0.98) + 0.01*log(0.01) + 0.01*log(0.01)] = 0.11

B --> -1* [0.33*log(0.33) + 0.33*log(0.33) + 0.33*log(0.33)] = 1.09

B is the one with the highest uncertainty, the numbers are not tiny and we don't have problems anymore with p=0. So it looks like we achieved our goal !

the general form of the formula is

Interpretation

The easiest way to interpret this quantity is to tweak a bit the formula. In fact the formula can be written like so:

These formulas are equivalents because:

$latex log(\frac{1}{p}) = log(1) - log(p) = -log(p) &fg=000000&bg=ffffff&s=1$

Then this looks an awful lot like an expected value. Recall that the general formula for the expected value is.

$latex ExpectedValue(X) = \sum_{i=1} ^{n} x_{i} \times p_{i} &fg=000000&bg=ffffff&s=1$

Where x in our context is the uncertainty $latex log(\frac{1}{p} ) &fg=000000&bg=ffffff&s=1$.

If you are not used to expected values, you can just see it as a weighted average.

In conclusion, you can see the entropy as the expected uncertainty of the distribution (the weighted average of the uncertainty) in the distribution, it helps you answer the question "How uncertain my distribution is ?".

Further explanation

Let's take a closer look of what we have done previously, when you tried to build the formula from scratch. To do so we make things even simpler and compute the uncertainty in the case of two possibilities, that will make us able to plot it on a graph. Indeed, in the case of two possibilities when you choose the first probability p then the other is (1-p).

In this context, the product of the probabilities is p(1-p)

We can see that the plot increases from x=0 up until x=0.5 then it decreases. This is what we expected, if the probabilities are equally distributed then p = 0.5 and (1-p) = 0.5 thus the uncertainty is at its peak. Also, the graph is obviously symmetric because if p = 0.2 then (1-p) = 0.8, it's the same as p = 0.8 and (1-p) = 0.2

When we apply the log we get log(p(1-p)) = log(p) + log(1-p) all the values become negatives but the relations of order are preserved, the function reaches its maximum for x=0.5 like previously. The only issue is that the functions tends to -infinity when x approaches 0 or 1.

multiplying all the terms with their probabilities leads to plog(p) + (1-p)log(1-p). As seen previously, it changes the relations of order. The reason is that it forces the function to be equal to 0 for the values x = 0 and x = 1 which flips the graph. Also, all the other values are lowered because they are being multiplied by their probability which are numbers smaller than 1.

So we just multiply the whole thing by -1 to get what we want.

you can use whatever base you want for the log, if you choose the log base 2 then you can say that the results are in bits and the maximum value that the function can take is 1.

I still don't understand why there is a logarithmic function in the Shannon entropy formula ?

There are at least 3 good reasons :

  • It is suitable when dealing with huge or tiny numbers. For instance
    $latex log_{2}(100 000)= 16.6 &fg=000000&bg=ffffff&s=1$ , which makes the output much more practical.

  • It coincides with Gibbs entropy) formula used in thermodynamics, and very often it is useful in science to link concepts between disciplines in order to make analogies.

  • The formula has some interesting additive properties. Feel free to read Shannon’s original paper if you are interested to know more about this topic.

How is Shanon Entropy different from variance, where is it used ?

  • They both measure information but entropy is all about probabilities, that is to say you are trying to characterize a probability distribution, it doesn't care about the values themselves. This is interesting because you can compute the entropy of any categorical data which can't be done with variance. This works even if the data is non numerical, example: ["one", "one", "two", "one"]
  • Entropy is used in Machine Learning, especially in Decision trees as an impurity criterion. the Decision tree splits the data at each node using impurity. The goal here is to choose the feature that minimizes the impurity. When the impurity is low it means that most of the labels are correctly predicted, in other words the uncertainty is very low. You keep adding nodes until the impurity doesn't decrease anymore. Note that this Idea goes with the previous point, the entropy trick makes the decision trees able to deal with numerical and categorical datas.

How to use Entropy in Python ?

There is a method in scipy that computes entropy but it doesn’t take an array of labels as input, it takes an array of probabilities instead. So you have to compute first the probabilities associated with each label before using the entropy method from scipy.

[code language="python"]# Get probabilities associated with every label import numpy as np labels = [0,0,1,1,1] values, counts = np.unique(labels, return_counts=True) probs = counts / len(labels) print("values:", values) print("counts:", counts) print("probs:", probs) #>>> values: [0, 1] #>>> counts: [2, 3] #>>> probs: [0.4, 0.6][/code]

Now, we can plug probs in the entropy method. The original formula uses the log base 2 because communication/ information was thought in terms of bits but you can choose whatever base you want.

[code language="python"]from scipy.stats import entropy e = entropy(probs, base=2) print(e) #>>> 0.9709505944546688[/code]

Finally we can define a function that takes a list of labels as input and returns its shannon entropy.

[code language="python"]from scipy.stats import entropy def entropy_from_labels(labels, base=2): """Take a list of labels as input and return its shannon entropy""" value, counts = np.unique(labels, return_counts=True) probs = counts/len(labels) return entropy(probs, base=base) entropy_from_labels(labels, base=2) #>>> 0.9709505944546688[/code]

item.title: Understanding projections - They are everywhere in Machine Learning !
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
These days I felt like writing an article about projections. Simply because I noticed that projections are one of these mathematical tools that people daily use without even realizing it.

I'll try to make things clear by going step by step but I assume you have some remembrance of high school level maths and some basic notions of linear algebra. Hopefully this article won't be to difficult to read.

Scalar projection of a vector

Let's use a practical situation to describe a projection. Let's say that for some reason, someone is trapped on top of a leaning pole. He asks you to put a mattress on the ground so that he can safely jump on it.

The problem is that you are not exactly sure where to put the mattress. That's where projections come into action.

In a sense, yo can see it as measuring the shadow of the leaning pole, caused by the sunlight that casts rays perpendicular to the ground. That's what we call an orthogonal projection.

Before jumping into the problem, I would like to be clear about some basic notations.
let a be a data point that has two coordinates x=3 and y=4.
then, knowing these coordinates, the data point is fully defined and you can put a(3,4) on the graph.

But the same coordinates are also useful to define not the data point anymore but the vector.
You can differentiate them with the little arrow above the a.

These two guys are defined the same way but they are not exactly the same mathematical object.

Firstly, this is interesting to note that a(3,4) is sufficient to define the object a as a vector because we are working with position vectors and such vectors always starts at the origin (0,0). So when we write a(3,4) we implicitly say that this vector starts from (0,0) and goes to the point (3,4).

There are several ways you can intepret vectors but for now let's just stick with the basic way to see it:
It's an object that has a magnitude and points towards a direction.

So we can use this vector a(3,4) to model our leaning pole.

Also note that i is the unit vector that points towards the point (1,0).
It is called a unit vector because its norm or magnitude is 1.

So here is to problem, knowing that the leaning pole's height is 5m and that it points towards the point (3,4), what is the distance d ?

the answer is quite immediate with a little bit of high school math.
the answer is $latex d = hcos \theta &fg=000000&bg=ffffff&s=1$

  • also h is just the magnitude of the vector a which can be written |a|
  • $latex cos \theta &fg=000000&bg=ffffff&s=1$ can be written using the dot product between a and i.

generally, you can see a dot product being written <a, i> or $latex a^T.i &fg=000000&bg=ffffff&s=1$ or even just a.i.
I'will use the linear algebra notation which is $latex a^T.i &fg=000000&bg=ffffff&s=1$

So the distance d can now simply be written:

And now you can see why it's interesting to take a unit vector, because the final expression becomes so simple ! The projection of a on i is just the dot product of a and i

And as you might have guessed (because the example is actually trivial) the result is 3

Note that the dot product of two vector is always a scalar. Interestingly in french the dot product is called a "produit scalaire" because it is the product of two vectors that returns a scalar.

So we just have to put the mattress on the x axis (on the ground) and put it 3m away from the leaning pole so this gentleman can safely jump.

Vector projection of a vector

Now, sometimes we don't really care about just having a scalar as a final output.
Instead we want the result as a vector which means having the coordinates of the projected point.

To do so, we can simply associate the scalar d with the direction of i.
This is simply done with the product d.i

now you get the projection as a vector (you can check on the graph that the answer is correct).
Basically what we have done is that we transformed a magnitude into a vector by giving this magnitude a direction.

This operation is called an outer product, like a dot product, an outer product involves two vectors.
In our case d can be seen as a 1x1 vector.

Projection of a Matrix

Now things are becoming interesting ! What if we didn't have only one vector to project onto u but 2 and we wanted to do all the projection with a single operation ? This is what matrices are made for !

Let's get back to the original graph with an extra vector b

We can then stack the vectors into a matrix called A

This way, we can perform the dot product with u for each line of the matrix (for each vector).

We end up with the projection of a and b onto u (i becomes u because it's just more handy to have a unit vector called u). These are wrapped up in the output vector. As seen previously these scalars 3 and 4 are the magnitudes of the projections.

Now let's give those magnitudes a direction with the outer product so they can become vectors.

As a conclusion, if u is a unit vector these simple formulas can get vectors projected !

  • for a vector a onto u : $latex a.u.u^T &fg=000000&bg=ffffff&s=1$
  • for a matrix A onto u : $latex A.u.u^T &fg=000000&bg=ffffff&s=1$

Note if the vector you are projecting on is not normalized, you can normalize it by dividing it with its norm !

A less trivial example (but still easy)

Now let's take an example where the vector you are projecting on is less trivial and doesn't have a magnitude of 1.

First, let's normalize this bad boy v.

We'll now use u which points towards the same direction than v but has a magnitude of 1.

The projection of a on u is written $latex p_u(a) &fg=000000&bg=ffffff&s=1$

We can see on the graph that the projected vector is indeed (2.5, 2.5)

Projections are ubiquitous in Machine Learning

Projections are all over the place in ML, especially in the linear models like PCA or Linear Regression. Previously what I've explained in that a matrix A can be projected on a vector u just with a matrix multiplication A.u.

Does it ring a bell ?

If it doesn't let's take a closer look at how we can interpret A.u.

Remember that we can interpret a matrix as a stacking of data points/vectors (rows) or a stacking of features (columns).

A.u can be written like so

This can now be read as a linear combination of the columns. Everytime we multiply a matrix with a vector, we are calculating a weighted sum of the columns, the weights being the coefficients in the vector.

Now this should explain a lot of things as linear combinations are ubiquitous in ML.

Indeed, think about PCA where we are looking for the linear combination of the features/columns that maximizes variance. In fact this linear combination X.u is just the projection of X on u. If we rephrase it, we are looking for a vector u so that the projection of X on u has the highest possible variance.

In a sense, we could say that linear combinations and projections are "cousins".

That's all for today folks !

item.title: Understanding decorators in Python with a case study
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
What are decorators ?

Today, I would like to speak about decorators. This is quite an advanced technique in Python but you'll see that it's not a very difficult concept to understand and once you master it, it will really improve your code quality, making it more concise, more understandable and even faster in some cases.

So what are these fellow decorators ?

You may have encountered while reading some code a function definition with a fancy @ above. Like so:

[code language="python"]@decorator #<-- this is a decorator def func(): #do something[/code]

It may seem very weird but it's actually no big deal. A decorator is a function that takes a function as input and returns another function that is able to do new things. It's like enhancing or giving new super powers to an existing function, got it ? :)

[code language="python"]def my_decorator(input_func): #do something with input_func return output_func[/code]

To use it in a more convenient way there is this special syntax:

[code language="python"]@my_decorator def func(): #do something[/code]

And this is it you are good to go !

Well not quite yet, first let's get back to the previous definition and let's elaborate a bit on it because there is something important to understand.

As you are returning a new function that didn't exist before (output_func), it means that you need to define it inside the decorator my_decorator like so:

[code language="python"]def my_decorator(input_func): def output_func(): #do something with input_func input_func(...) return output_func[/code]

If you are not used to nested function it might seem weird but in fact it's a very common thing to define a function inside another one.

Case Study - map function with multiple arguments

Do you now the function called map ? It applies a function to each element of an iterable. Here is an example:

[code language="python"]int_list = [2, 3, 4] my_func = lambda x: x**2 map(my_func, int_list) #>>> map at 0x1069aa400> #it returns a map object. list(map(my_func, int_list)) #let's convert it to a list to see the result #>>> [4, 9, 16][/code]

Now the thing is that map doesn't allow you to handle multiple function arguments. If my_func has to take multiple inputs, this just can't work. An example bellow:

[code language="python"]my_list = [('a', 'b'), ('c', 'd')] def concat(x, y): return x+y list(map(concat, my_list)) #>>> TypeError: () missing 1 required positional argument: 'y'[/code]

What's happening here is that each tuple of the list is interpreted as one argument. It's basically like trying to execute this line:

[code language="python"]concat(x= ('a', 'b')) # we want concat(x='a', y='b') instead[/code]

We want to somehow unpack the tuples inside the function concat beforehand. To do so, we could create a function that unpacks tuples.

[code language="python"]my_list = [('a', 'b'), ('c', 'd')] def concat(x, y): return x+y def unpacker(items): return concat(*items) #the start operator * unpacks the tuple list(map(unpacker, my_list)) #>>> ['ab', 'cd'][/code]

It does work fine but there are many reasons not to code it this way.

  • Firstly, when you read the code map(unpacker, my_list) it's not very clear that you are applying a function that does concatenations. You don't want to make your code implicit.

  • Secondly, the unpacker function is very specific, its only job is to unpack tuples for the concat function.Instead you would want such a function to be more generic so you can use it for other functions, not only concat.

  • ...

To define a more generic unpacker we can use decorators !

[code language="python"]#define the decorator def unpacker(func): #creating a nested function to unpack args for `func` def star_func(args): #unpack args return func(*args) #return the new function return star_func @unpacker def _concat(x, y): return x+y list(map(_concat, my_list)) #>>> ['ab', 'cd'][/code]

Isn't it beautiful ? :)

the function _concat now has the ability to unpack the input arguments ! :). Also this is done in a very clean fashion, very little code and eveything is explicit. Moreover if I need to do this for another function, I can just use @unpacker above it !

As a final exercice we can definie a function starmap that uses map as core function and that can handle multiple arguments.

[code language="python"]def starmap(func, iterable): """apply map on an iterable where each element of this iterable is a tuple""" #_func derives from func, it just unpacks arguments beforehand. @unpacker def _func(*args): return func(*args) return map(_func, iterable) list(starmap(concat, my_list)) #>>> ['ab', 'cd'][/code]

If you prefer you can code it this way. It's slightly more compact but it may seem weird for someone used to decorators :D .

[code language="python"]def starmap(func, iterable): """apply map on an iterable where each element of this iterable is a tuple""" _func = unpacker(func) return map(_func, iterable) list(starmap(concat, my_list)) #>>> ['ab', 'cd'][/code]

Keep in mind this exercice was made for pedagogical purpose, it may not be the most straight forward way to code a starmap function. If you ever need to use map with multiple arguments, I recommand you to use the starmap function from itertools

Some decorators to know

@cache and @lru_cache:
Most recent calls are cached in a dictionnary. It can save time when using a function that periodically calls same arguments.

[code language="python"]from functools import lru_cache @lru_cache def factorial(n): return n * factorial(n-1) if n else 1[/code]

@classmethod
Another built in decorator! Once again the name says it all. It allows you
to define a method or a function that is not associated with an instance but with
the class itself. So as a reference argument we use cls that stands for class
rather than self that is used to symbolize an instance.

[code language="python"]class MyClass: @classmethod #we use cls as it stands for class rather than self that symbolizes the instance. def my_class_method(cls, x, y): return x + y #Notice that i didn't create any instance beforehand. MyClass.my_class_method(1, 2) #>>> 3 #Of course you can also access this method with an instance of the class. instance = MyClass() instance.my_class_method(1, 2) #>>> 3[/code]

@staticmethod
This is a built in decorator, it is widely used when defining methods inside a class. Its use is to flag functions that are static as its name suggests. A function is static when it doesn't interact with other functions or attributes of the class. You can see that a function is static when self is not used at all inside its definition.

In fact, a staticmethod can't have cls or self as parameter nor it can access class atributes or instance attributes.

A staticmethod is kind of a very lonely function that is not able to interact with anyone or anything excepts its arguments :D

[code language="python"]class MyClass: my_attribute = 0 @staticmethod #note that it didn't have to put `self` as an argument. def my_static_method(x,y): return x + y #This function is dynamic as it interacts with an attribute of the instance. def my_dynamic_method(self, x, y): self.my_attribute = x + y return self.my_attribute #note that for a dynamic method i have to put `self` as an argument but #it feels weird as it's not using any attribute or method of the instance. def my_weird_method(self, x, y): return x + y instance = MyClass() instance.my_static_method(1,2) #>>>3[/code]

@app.route in Flask
This decorator is very important when using the framework Flask. It's designed to tell Flask what URL should trigger the function you are defining. Similarly there is @app.get for FastAPI.

[code language="python"]from flask import Flask app = Flask(__name__) @app.route("/my_url") def hello_world(): return "

Hello, World!

" #suppose the url to your website is www.mywebsite.com #when you'll go to www.mywebsite.com/my_url it will trigger the function `hello_world`[/code]

item.title: Cosine similarity: an Intuitive and simple explanation
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Cosine similarity is one of the most important metric in Natural Language Processing. It is most often used to quantify a distance between two embeddings (or 2 vectors). As embeddings are supposed to gather semantic information, the cosine similarity between two embeddings becomes somewhat a semantic distance.

If you are not familiar with this metric in ML and you just heard of the cosine from high school, you may wonder what the hell the adjacent side over the hypotenuse on a right triangle has to do with vectors and similarities :D . You'll see in this article that the cosine serves different purposes.

As always in Machine Learning and especially in Linear Algebra, it's always good to use simple examples in order to understand concepts, generally, you'll be able to generalize the reasoning afterwards. In Linear algebra, whenever it's possible, I recommand you to build your inuition in 2 dimensions first, simply because you can plot 2D vectors on a graph so you can visualize what's going on.

The question we are going to answer is "what is the cosine of two vectors on 2D ?", but before let met introduce you the idea behind the cosine measure. In fact, it's a very simple concept, you just want to know if 2 vectors point towards the same direction. Indeed, if it's the case well you can say that the vectors are very similar, otherwise if they are perpendicular, they are very different.

Before considering the cosine itself, an intuitive way to determine if 2 vectors points to the same direction is to measure the angle between them.

Let's examine these cases:

  • in the first example, the vectors u and v point towards the same direction, the angle between them is 0°. the vectors can't be more similar, in this case, the similarity is equal to 1.
  • in the second example, the vectors u and v are perpendicular, they form an angle of 90°, they can't be more different than that. In this case the similarity is equal to 0
  • in the last example. the angle between u and v is a bit less than 45°. In this case the similarity lays between 0 and 1 (the result is quite close to 1 though.)

By looking at the first example, we should realize that if we are only interested in directions then the magnitude of the vectors don't matter. So why don't we just get rid of the magnitudes and see if it doesn't simplify the problem ? To do so, it's very simple, we just have to divide the vectors by their respective norms so they become unit vectors.

  • In the first example, Now u and v have the same magnitude and point towards the same direction, they are identical. Note that if we were to project v on u the magnitude of the projected vector would be the same as the magnitude of v which is 1.

  • In the second example, if we were to project u on v, the projected vector would have a magnitude of 0.

  • In the third example, the projection of u on v would have a magnitude of +/- 0.89.

Wait a minute, instead of calculating an angle between two vectors, can't we just calculate a projection? The answer is yes :) and this is exactly what is a cosine but don't tell anybody.

So here is the key takeway: measuring the angle between the vectors is closely related to measuring the magnitude of the projected vector (if u and v are unit vectors). You can visualize in the animation bellow that the magnitude of the projection decreases as the angle between the vectors increases.

Note: as long as you are working with unit vectors, it doesn't matter if you project u on v or v on u, the result is the same.

So in fact the cosine similarity is all about calculating the projection of a vector on another when these have a magnitude of 1. Luckily it's very easy to calculate it, it's just a dot product. Please read my blog post about projections if you don't feel confortable with this assertion.

Note: $latex P_v(u) &fg=000000&bg=ffffff&s=1$ stands for projection of u on v.

You can always make a vector have a magnitude of 1 by dividing it by its norm. so the formula that always work to calculate a cosine it the following one.

In fact, you can see a cosine as a normalized version of a dot product.

Let's get more concrete with a simple example.

Up until now, theses vectors remained somewhat abstract. Now suppose that you have two documents u and v, for each one you want to know if it deals with cats or dogs. So for each document you'll count the number of repetitions of the words "cat" and "dog".

  • In the first example, on document u, the frequency of cat is 2 while the frequency of dog is 0, thus we can say that the document is all about cats. On document v it's also all about cats with a frequency of 4. In that regards both documents are similar in the sense that the topic is the same.In this case, the similarity is equal to 1. The word cat could have a frequency of 900, it won't change the fact that it's all about cats, this is why the magnitude of the vector doesn't matter, we only need the normalized version of it or in other words, we only need the direction of the vectors.

  • In the second example, u is all about dogs while v is all about cats, the documents can't be any different thus the similarity is 0, this is the case where the vectors are perpendicular.

  • In the third example, u is mostly about cats and a bit about dogs while v is all about cats. The documents are still a lot similar, the value of the similarity if you were to compute the cosine is 0.89.

By now, I hope you can get a more pragmatic sense of what having the same direction for two vectors really means. In fact it means that the vectors (or the documents if you want to be more concrete) have similar ratios or distribution across the features.

That's it for this small article folks :) , I hope it helped you getting a sense of what the cosine is and why we use it as a measure of similarity in NLP.

item.title: Deploy a sentence transformer model on AWS Lambda via Docker
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Today, let's dive into the beautiful (and sometimes very painful) world of deployment.

This is really when things start to be very exciting as a you generally go from a model in a notebook to a product/service that can be delivered to users :) . At the same time a lot of things can go wrong during the process, so it's really important to be organized and to stay focused !

We are going to deploy a sentence transformer model on AWS lambda via Docker. This post covers most of the needs but won't dive too much into advanced details otherwise it won't be a blog post anymore but a full deployment course.

Prerequisites

To follow this tutorial, you should:

  • have Docker installed and know the basics.
  • have an AWS account
  • have AWS-CLI installed
  • know the basic bash commands
  • be familiar with Python
  • be familiar with Python virtual environments

Yes, you should know quite a lot of things already, uh ? :)

Link to the Github repo

You can find all the files used in this blog post on my Github repo

Few words about Lambda

To briefly introduce AWS Lambda, it is a compute service that lets you run code without provisioning or managing servers. In other words you provide the code and AWS takes care of the rest.

Lambda can be used without Docker but AWS let you package and deploy Lambda functions as container images of up to 10GB in size ! This is very useful when dealing with sentence transformers because they can be very heavy !

Create a virtual environment

I highly recommand you to create a new python environments each time you are working on a new project. A virtual environment is a tool that helps to keep dependencies required by different projects separate by creating isolated python virtual environments for them.

The most critical thing is perhaps to keep track of the versions of the different packages used. Let say you don't work with virtual environments, you built your app A with pytorch version x, then you are working on another app B that requires pytorch version y, you go back to app A Using pytorch version y, this can make the whole app crash or even worse, it may continue to work but with differences in the outputs which makes the debbuging very difficult.

Every single thing that can reduce head scratching in deployment is very welcome.

create an environment with python 3.7 using the terminal :

python3.7 -m venv <name_of_your_env>

or

python3.7 -m virtualenv <name_of_your_env>

once created you can activate the environnment like so:

source <name_of_your_env>/bin/activate

later on, if you need to deactivate your environment, you can use the following command:

deactivate

Choose your sentence transformer model

You can try a lot of different models provided by HuggingFace, you have to find the best compromise between model size and performances for your use case. Note that some of the models are multilingual some are not, I highly recommand you to read the documentation of each model before using it.

For the sake of simplicity I will be using one of the tiniest model : all-MiniLM-L6-v2, it weights 80 Mb.

One you chose your model, you can quickly use it, it's very simple. Just install the sentence transformers library like so :

[code language="bash"]pip install -U sentence-transformers[/code]

and then

[code language="python"]from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer # The first time you run this line, it will download and install the chosen model. model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2') sentences = ['This framework generates embeddings for each input sentence', 'Sentences are passed as a list of string.', 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.'] sentence = 'This is my input sentence' # Sentences are encoded by calling model.encode() embeddings = model.encode(sentences) # See how the model can also take as input a text rather than a list of texts. embedding = model.encode(sentence) print(embeddings.shape) print(embedding.shape) #>>> (3, 384) #>>> (384,)[/code]

The output embeddings is a numpy array of shape (3, 384). The first element of the shape 3 refers to the number of sentences in the input list. Then each sentence is being vectorized by the model in a space of 384 dimensions, which is why the second element of the shape is 384.

In the same fashion, embedding is a numpy array of shape (384,). There's only one element in the tuple as the input is a string, not a list of strings. It would have had a shape of (1, 384) if the input was wrapped in a list.

The key takeways here are :

  • The first time you use a model, it will automatically be downloaded (we have to keep this in mind for the deployment)
  • The input for the model can be a text or a list of texts, depending on this, the output's shape will be different.

Now that you've carefully chosen the model that better suits your use case, let's make a simple app.

Code your app

The core module is generally named app.py. Inside this module, the core function is conventionally named lambda_handler, this is the function that will be used by AWS Lambda. This very function has some constraints to satisfy. Indeed, it must have two arguments event and context, we don't have to worry too much about context however event is where the input should be located. event has to be a dictionnary, this is mandatory because of the way Lambda functions work (they expect a JSON as input and return a JSON as output).

A part from that, there's no particular constraints to point out, at least for now. :)

In our case we design a very simple input of the following form:

[code language="javascript"]event = {"my_input": my input sentence...}[/code]
[code language="python"]# app.py file from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer model_name = 'all-MiniLM-L6-v2' model = SentenceTransformer(model_name) def my_app(my_input): """Simple app that tranforms text(s) into vector(s) using a sentence transformer model""" output = model.encode(my_input) return output def lambda_handler(event:dict, context:str): # unpacking my_input. my_input = event['my_input'] # using the transformer model. # don't forget to convert the numpy array to list so it can be JSON Serializable. output = my_app(my_input).tolist() return output[/code]

We can't make a simpler app than that :) .

  • my_app just uses the encode method of the sentence transformer, in order to casually transform the input into embeddings.
  • lambda_handler is simply a wrapper for my_app, in fact, it does the same thing but is slightly different so it can suit the way Lambda functions are designed (JSON & context in, JSON out).

If you were wondering, actually it doesn't have a lot of use to make such an app, I just want to avoid writing code as much as possible, for this tutorial. The main motivation here is to give you a template you can adapt.

Make requirements.txt

A useful command to know is :

[code language="bash"]pip freeze>requirements.txt[/code]

This will create in your directory a file named requirements.txt with all the packages used in a particular environment. If you don't want to bother, this can be a very quick way to make requirements.

in our case, we can make things even simpler as the only package installed is sentence-transformers. You'll also need huggingface-hub, for some reason this lib is not automatically installed with sentence-transformers despite beeing a dependency. Lastly we use a cpu only version of torch to make its size smaller and because there's no GPU available with lambda.

[code language="bash"]#requirements.txt file https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu/torch-1.10.1%2Bcpu-cp37-cp37m-linux_x86_64.whl huggingface-hub==0.11.1 sentence-transformers==2.2.2[/code]

Make DockerFile

The DockerFile is where we have to list informations about how to build the Docker image. We want our Image to:

  • be able to execute python scripts
  • to contain our app and requirements
  • but also to contain the sentence transformer model beforehand.

Remember we used the model all-MiniLM-L6-v2, remember also that if an environment doesn't contain the desired model, it will be automatically downloaded ...

Knowing that an instance of the image is created each time there is a user request, it would be absolutely disastrous if the model is downloaded again and again each time. To avoid it we have to specify in the DockerFile where to download the model, this way it will be available inside the image without the need to redownload it.

you can browse this webpage to find all the models of HuggingFace. Our model can be reached via this link https://public.ukp.informatik.tu-darmstadt.de/reimers/sentence-transformers/v0.2/all-MiniLM-L6-v2.zip

The DockerFile should look like this.

[code language="yaml"]# Dockerfile # We install python 3.7 from the AWS repository FROM public.ecr.aws/lambda/python:3.7 # Set environment variable ENV_NAME = Docker, you'll understand why we do it in a moment. ENV ENV_NAME Docker # Copy app.py and requirements.txt in the Docker Image we are building. COPY app.py requirements.txt ./ # Upgrade pip if needed RUN python -m pip install --upgrade pip # Install Sentence Transformer and other dependencies in requirements.txt RUN pip3 install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt --default-timeout=2000 # Create the directory 'model' RUN mkdir -p ./model # Download the sentence-transfomer model and put it in the directory './model' RUN curl https://public.ukp.informatik.tu-darmstadt.de/reimers/sentence-transformers/v0.2/all-MiniLM-L6-v2.zip -o ./model/all-MiniLM-L6-v2.zip # Unzip the model RUN unzip ./model/all-MiniLM-L6-v2.zip -d ./model/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 # Delete the zip file as we don't need it anymore RUN rm ./model/all-MiniLM-L6-v2.zip # Give full access to the dir so that it won't trigger the error permission denied in AWS Lambda # "[Errno 13] Permission denied: './all-MiniLM-L6-v2/modules.json'", RUN chmod -R 644 ./model RUN chmod -R 755 ./model #The CMD command​ specifies the instruction that is to be executed when a Docker container starts. CMD ["app.lambda_handler"][/code]

Adapt app.py

At this point your folder should look like this

[code language="bash"]# your project folder should look like this ├── Dockerfile # Dockerfile ├── requirements.txt # pip requirements └── app.py # the core module[/code]

When the Docker container is built, it would look like this.

[code language="bash"]# When The Docker container is built, it would look like this ├── requirements.txt # pip requirements ├── app.py # the core module └── model # directory with the sentence-transformer model └── all-MiniLM-L6-v2 # the sentence-transformer model[/code]

We have to slightly adapt the code in app.py in order to use a sentence transformer model from a local path. If you read the documentation, you'll find out that instead of passing the model name to load it, you can directly pass the path to the model directory.

Parameters: model_name_or_path – If it is a filepath on disc, it loads the model from that path. If it is not a path, it first tries to download a pre-trained SentenceTransformer model. If that fails, tries to construct a model from Huggingface models repository with that name.

the problem is that this parameter changes depending on the environment we work in.

  • When we work locally we have to use model_name_or_path = 'all-MiniLM-L6-v2'
  • When we work in the Docker environment we have to use model_name_or_path = 'model/all-MiniLM-L6-v2'

how to distinguish between environments ?
That's where the previous environment variable ENV_NAME defined in the DockerFile comes into action. Everything becomes clearer it the snippet bellow.

[code language="python"]# app.py file from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer import os # Check if the environment variable ENV_NAME is set and equal to 'Docker' # Otherwise if it's not set, we are working locally, we don't need to pass the path to the model. if os.environ.get('ENV_NAME') == 'Docker': model_name_or_path = 'model/all-MiniLM-L6-v2' os.environ['TRANSFORMERS_CACHE'] = './model' else: model_name_or_path = 'all-MiniLM-L6-v2' model = SentenceTransformer(model_name_or_path) def my_app(my_input): """Simple app that tranforms text(s) into vector(s) using a sentence transformer""" output = model.encode(my_input) return output def lambda_handler(event:dict, context:str): # unpacking my_input my_input = event['my_input'] # don't forget to convert the numpy array to list so it can be JSON Serializable output = my_app(my_input).tolist() return output[/code]

This simple tweak is very handy because the same code can be run locally or in the Docker environment !

Build the Docker Image

Allright, an important step is now to build the Docker image.

[code language="bash"]docker build -t my_transformer_app .[/code]

Test the Docker Image

Once your image is up and running, you can test it with the following tip.

First, in a new terminal window run your docker container. This will run a local server.

[code language="bash"]docker run -p 9000:8080 my_transformer_app[/code]

In your original terminal window you can then send a request like so.

[code language="bash"]curl -XPOST "http://localhost:9000/2015-03-31/functions/function/invocations" -d '{"my_input": "hello world"}'[/code]

By doing this, we are sending a Json to the server created by docker with the input "hello world" inside but you can pass whatever string you want. If everything works correctly, you'll get a nice vector back :)

Going online

What are we going to do now ?

We are going to push the Dockerized model into ECR, then we'll create our lambda function from the container image, this is as simple as that !

Push your Docker Image to AWS ECR

ECR (Elastic Container Registery) is an AWS managed container image registry, we are going to use it in order to push our image.

  • Go to the Amazon ECR console .
  • If it's the first time you access the console, Choose Get Started, for Visibility settings, choose Private.
  • If it's not, you can go ahead and click on the button Create repository

In order to make things simpler, make the repository name the same as the name of the Docker Image. You can leave all the other settings as is.

You can finish the creation of the repository by hitting the Create repository button.

Your repository is now up and running. Finally, you simply have to hit the View push commands button and follow the instructions in order to push your image.

It may take some minutes before it's done, be patient ! At the end of the process, when you refresh the page you can see your image with all its information displayed.

That's it for this part :)

Create your Lambda function using the Docker Image.

Creating a function with Lambda takes only few minutes:

  • Open the function page of the lambda console.
  • Choose Create function
  • Select Container image
  • Enter a function name
  • Click Browse Images and choose the image you've just created

Configure ressources

If everything went as expected, you should end up having this function overview.

Now that your function is created, you have to configure the amount of ressources (CPU, RAM...) it needs to run properly.

  • Click Configuration in the navigation bar
  • Choose General configuration
  • Then Edit

  • The heavier the sentence transformer model is, the more ressources and computation time it requires. In my case, because the model is very tiny, 512 mb of RAM is allright, but sometimes you'll need 2,3 or maybe 4GB of RAM, only for the setence transformer model, I'm not even including other objects stored in the memory (other libraries, variables, data...). If you have no idea how much RAM you need, you can perform tests in order to establish it. As a very approximate rule of thumb, the RAM you need should be at least 4 x the size of your sentence transformer model. Keep in mind AWS let you allocate up to 10 GB of RAM.

  • Note that the CPU is automatically set by AWS, the function is allocated CPU proportional to the RAM configured.

  • Tiemout is also important to configure, in my case setting timeout to 30 sec does the job but again you have to determine the value by performing tests.

  • You can leave Execution Role as is, configuring roles are useful when you need to give your function access to other AWS ressources (S3, Redshift, SNS ...) or in the contrary to limit them, which is not our case.

Test the deployed lambda function

AWS provides a test interface. you can access it by clicking Test in the navigation bar. A test event is always a JSON input to your function.

Let's perform a very simple test, just so we can make sure everything runs properly.

[code language="javascript"]# Test event { "my_input": "hello hello" } `[/code]

The function runs ! It returned an embedding of a size of 384, the max memory used is 322 MB and the computation time is 10 seconds.

Again, you can find all the files used in this blog post on my Github repo.

And voila ! Congratulations for making it this far 8-) 8-) 8-) ! I hope you've found this tutorial useful !

item.title: Intuitive explanation of bayes theorem - Part 1/2
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
One of the most important formula in statistics is perhaps the bayes theorem.

Many people see this formula as somewhat magical and struggle to understand its math or getting the intuition of what's going on. In fact, once you understand it, it may seem very trivial and I suspect that teachers don't spend the time needed to really dive into it, instead they just give the formula and ask you to know it by heart. As the formula is quite simple, students find it easy to memorize and don't really spend time to get into it either. Knowing a formula by heart may be useful to pass exams but it won't help you in your scientist journey :) In the contrary, understanding the underlining concept will make you able to derive the formula instead of memorizing it.

I personnaly like to spend time on "easy" and "trivial" things because I consider them as the most important. Furthermore, there are many ML models and concepts built on top of the bayes rule so I garantee you that the time spent is worth it.

Without wasting any more time, let's begin !

Conditional probabilities

As Bayes theorem is all about conditionnal probabilities, we need to understand first what is a conditionnal probability (wink wink captain obvious).

Let's consider a population of cars in your neighborhood.
Suppose that the distribution of the colors is like so:

red cars: 30
blue cars: 50
black cars: 100
yellow cars: 20
TOTAL: 200

If I ask you the question what's the probability of seeing a blue car within your neighborhood, you would answer:
P(blue car) = 50/200 = 1/4
This is a probability in its most simple form, it is simply a way to quantify how likely something is to happen.

What are conditional probabilities then ?

As their name suggest, it's when we are adding a condition or some may say a restriction.

Let's now add a condition: There are taxi drivers among your neighbors and in your city taxis can be either black or yellow. For now, we consider that the ensemble taxi is formed by yellow cars + black cars.
Now what is the probability of seeing a yellow car KNOWING that it's a taxi ?
This is written:
P(yellow car | taxi)
the vertical bar stands for "knowing that"

As the population is now restricted to only black and yellow cars we are no longer taking into account the whole population but only a subset. We answer the question "What's the amount of yellow cars within the taxis ?"
P(yellow car | taxi) = 20/ (20+100) = 1/6

Still pretty intuitive isn't it ?

The general form of a conditional probability can be written
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)
the character ∩ symbolizes the intersection, in our case A ∩ B = yellow cars ∩ taxis = yellow cars
and P(B) = P(taxi)

Once again conditional probabilities are nothing more than calculating probabilities on a subset of the population.

Let's stick with Taxis a bit more

In fact, not all yellow and black cars are taxis, to be fair taxis are also a subset of the ensemble yellow cars + black cars. To make things clearer let's use this little diagram.

Let's play a bit with conditionnal probabilites in a visual way.

If a car is at the same time a taxi and a yellow car then it belongs to taxis ∩ yellow cars and it visually corresponds to this:

If we want the probability of a car being a taxi knowing that's it's a yellow car then we simply take the subset of yellow cars and see among it what is the proportion of taxis. Visually, it would look like that:

Got it ?

Sometimes it's more interesting to have the probability the other way around, that is to say having the probability of a yellow car knowing it's a taxi. No problem, within the subset of the taxis, what is the proportion of yellow cars ?

Let's put those two bad boys together in a single image so that we can compare them easily :)

Notice how these two probabilities share the same quantity in the numerator. In a way we can say that P(Taxi | Yellow car) and P(Yellow car | Taxi) are in fact "the same quantity seen through different glasses".

  • P(Taxi | Yellow car) sees taxis ∩ yellow cars from yellow cars point of view
  • whereas P(Yellow car | Taxi) sees taxis ∩ yellow cars from Taxi point of view

To me this is the key point to understand ! From there, we are one step away from "discovering the bayes theorem".

Bayes Theorem

The idea of Bayes Theorem is to have a simple formula that links P(A | B) to P(B | A). This would be darn handy because in real life you sometimes have easily access to P(A | B) but your ultimate goal is to find P(B | A) so you want to be able to switch from one quantity to the other.

Let's get back to the previous image, what if we get rid of the denominators of each quantity ? To do so, we simply multiply each quantity with their denominator:

These quantities are now equal !

The last step is to divide each side by P(Yellow car)

Ladies and gentleman, I'm very happy to introduce you Bayes theorem :)
It's general form is :

Should I memorize the formula ?

Hello no ! If someday you forget the formula, just remember that the formula is designed to link P(A | B) with P(B | A) and that they share the same quantity P(A ∩ B) then the following steps are straight forwards as A ∩ B is equivalent to B ∩ A. I just used a little tip by introducing P(A) and P(B) in the equality.

An example

  • We know the proportion of yellow cars among the taxis: P(Yellow | Taxi) = 0.5
  • It is also given that 5% of the cars in the neighborhood are taxis.

What is the probability of a car being a taxi knowing that it's a yellow car (P(Taxi | Yellow)) ?

Let's solve this

Let's calculate first the numerator and the denominator of the formula.

Numerator = P(Yellow | Taxi) x P(Taxi)= 0.5 x 0.05
Denominator = P(Yellow) = 20/200 = 0.1

Finally,
P(Taxi | Yellow) = N/D = 0.5 x 0.05 / 0.1 = 0.25

P(Taxi | Yellow) = 25%

Extended version of the formula

Sometimes you'll see the bayes formula used with a longer denominator. In fact it's still the same formula, it's just an "extended version".

Consider this situation:

we divided Taxi into two new groups: big taxis and small taxis. in order to make it easier to write down things let's consider that:

  • big taxis = A1
  • small taxis = A2

A1 and A2 form a partition of the space Taxis. This means that the sum of A1 + A2 forms exactly Taxis, in other words there's no overlap between these two, or you can also say that they are mutually exclusive.

Now that you are confortable with the concept of partition, let's form a partition of Yellow cars.

Note that the c above Taxi in the last quantity stands for "not", i.e it represents all the cars that are not taxis.

Thus

Thus

To simplify writing let's say that not taxi = A3

Finally

Now let's apply bayes theorem to the probability of A1 given Yellow (P(A1 | Yellow)):

Let's plug into the formula the "extended version of P(Yellow)"

And voila !

The general form can be written like so:

Remember ! This holds true only if the events (A1,...,An) form a partition of the space, that is to say they are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive.

Merci ! This is the end of the article, I hope I made Bayes formula a little bit easier to understanded. :)

item.title: Intuitive explanation of bayes theorem – Part 2/2
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
In my previous article about Bayes theorem I attempted to explain in a simple way the main ideas behind the formula. Today, let's take it to another level! I'll show you a way that allows you to update your prior beliefs given new information. Some people call this way to use the Bayes Theorem the diachronic Bayes because it evolves through time with new information ! Indeed, you update your believes as you collect more evidence.

Recall the Bayes Theorem:

Now let's just chage a bit the notation and Introduce the notions of "hypothesis" and "Data" Let H be hypothesis and D be the Data, the formula becomes:

Note that it's not the "final form" of the formula, generally we expand the denominator so it can be calculated. Recall that in my previous blog post we used the law of total probability to expand it. The idea is to break P(D) into smaller pieces, I've prepared a little drawing to make it clearer (feel free to read my previous article if it's still not crystal clear).



The smaller pieces must form a partition of D which meach that they are mutually exclusives (no overlap between the pieces) and colletively exhaustive (the sum of the pieces equals D).

If you find these notations somewhat enigmatic for now, don't worry we will dive into an example shortly, hopefully it will be clearer.

Before that, I'd like to comment a bit each quantity of the Bayes formula.



P(H | D)

This is called the posterior probability because it's the result you get after applying the bayes theorem. It gives you the probability of the hypothesis given the Data. This quantity is equal to the Likelihood times Prior divided by the probability of the Data.

Generally we don't mention P(D) at all, instead we just say that P(H | D) is proportional to the Likelihood x Prior.



P(D)

This is the probability of the Data, This quantity might sound somewhat vague. As said before, we generally don't mention it at all because most of the time we don't actually need it (at least at first). We can notice that the denominator (which is P(D) ) in the "expanded" version of the Bayes theorem is in reality the same expression as the numerator.

The only difference is that It sums over all the possible hypothesis. So in fact when you calculated all the P(D | H_i)P(H_i) you can just sum them together and the result would be equal to P(D) (Again this is just the law of total probability). In fact, this quantity can be seen as a normalizing constant that makes all the probabilities add up to 1. In other words we don't really have to worry about P(D) and explicitly calculate it at first, you'll be able to find it a the last step of your calculation, you'll see in the example :) .

Note that this quantity can be very hard to calculate in some cases, especially for continuous variables that involve tricky distributions. That won't be the case in our example.



P(D | H)

This is called the likelihood because it is "how likely the Data is given the hypothesis" This is the easiest quantity you'll have to deal with.



P(H)

This is called the prior because it reflects your prior belief about the hypothesis. Generally this probability comes from the general knowledge or a study or sometimes it's only a subjective value which can be seen as prejudices. This is the reason why sometimes bayesian statistics are criticized and controversial.



Let's use the formula in an example

You are at a party and Bob would like too introduce you to some of his friends. Some of them have a bad reputation, they are konwn to be nasty. During the party you meet 3 groups of friends. Now the party is over, it's time to go home you decide to order an uber but you can't find your mobile phone. A kind person in the party comes to you and tells you that she saw someone dressed in black stealing your phone but she can't figure out exactly who this guy was.

Suppose that for each group of friends the people stayed together all party long which means they didn't mix up with other groups.

In the first group there were 3 people dressed in Black and 5 with other colors. In the second group there were 6 people dressed in Black and 5 with other colors In the third group there were 5 people dressed in Black and 4 with other colors

Group 1 --> B: 3 | O: 5
Group 2 --> B: 6 | O: 5
Group 3 --> B: 5 | O: 4

Also, you have no clue which group has done this, which means that each group has a priori the same probability of guilt

Which group has a posteriori the highest probability of containing the thief ?

Solution

Recall the formula:

We want to calculate the probability of the hypothesis given the Data

Here the hypothesis are:

  • H1: Group 1 is guilty
  • H2: Group 2 is guilty
  • H3: Group 3 is guilty

Let's calculate The probability associated with each hypothesis given the data so we can find the most probable scenario.

We have 2 quantities to really care about that is the likelihood P(D | H) and the prior P(H).

as each group has a priori the same probability of beeing guilty, the prior is distributed like so:

P(H = H1) = P(H = H2) = P(H = H3) = 1/3
(In the statistics lingo we also say that the variables are drawn from a uniform distribution.)

Now the likelihoods !

The likelihood is P(D | H). The idea here is to use the fact that the thief is dressed in black to evaluate how likely a group is to be guilty.

  • P(D = Black | H = Group 1) = 3/(3+5) = 0.38
  • P(D = Black | H = Group 2) = 6/(6+5) = 0.55
  • P(D = Black | H = Group 3) = 5(5+4) = 0.56





Now the work is almost done, we now have to multiply each Prior with its associated Likelihood.



As you can see in the column PxL (Prior times Likelihood) the values don't add up to one. If we want to address this problem we simply have to divide each value by the sum of this column. In fact the sum of all theses values equals to P(D), what we have named "the normalizing constant". This gives us the Posterior.

It turns out that group 2 and 3 have very close values



That data didn't help really...

But the nice thing about Diachronic Bayes is that you can save theses posterior probabilities somewhere and wait for new events. When you collect new data your prior distribution or belief won't be anymore 1/3, 1/3, 1/3 but it will be 0.26, 0.36, 0.38 as you gained new information with the data you gathered, in other words, you updated your believes.

Suppose now a friend of yours has experienced the same drama the day after you (yeah those people party every day :D ). After the party your friend comes to you and you have a talk. He somehow managed to have more accurate likelihoods, that is:

  • Group 1 Likelihood: 0.2
  • Group 2 Likelihood: 0.25
  • Group 3 Likelihood: 0.55

You decide to combine his information with yours. To be able to do that you take as a prior the posterior of your previous analysis and you associate it with the likelihoods of your friend.

Let's draw the posterior distribution



Okay... now that you gathered all the information you could get, the posterior distribution highly suggests that you should have a little talk with these nasty bad boys of the group 3 :D

Hopefully you now have a better understanding of how you can use Bayes Theorem in a diachronic way. This is the end of the article but there is still so much to talk about regarding Bayesian statistics. In particular Bayesian inference (how to predict new data), Bayesian networks (graphical models that represent probabilistic relationships between variables), Markov Chains Monte Carlo aka MCMC (allow for parameter estimation such as means, variances..., and exploration of tricky posterior distribution) but also the Naive Bayes Classifier (A machine learning model that uses Bayes Theorem).

item.title: Code Hack - How to render images inside a pandas DataFrame ? Super cool trick with an advanced bonus :)
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever wondered if there was an easy way too render images inside a pandas DataFrame ? How cool would it be to simply write down something like render_images(df) and that's it, that would do the trick for you ?

Today I'll show you a super cool trick to exactly do that ! Even better, I'll show you an "advanced technique" so that you could even do something like df.render_images(). In other words, you'll include the rendering function directly in the pd.DataFrame object :)



How to display an image in a notebook

First things first, the normal way to display images in notebooks is to use libraries like matplotlib, PIL, OpenCV etc... Let's go ahead with the PIL library to show a quick example.

[code language="python"]from PIL import Image path_to_img = 'images/standard_scaler_logo_black.jpg' # Create the image instance img = Image.open(path_to_img) # Here you can either use display(img) or img.show() display(img)[/code]

Now you can normally see a beautiful logo :) That being said, you can't really use these kind of libraries along with dataframes, they simply don't work together.

How to do then ? Well there's a cool module that is able to render html stuff that is IPython.core.display.HTML basically you provide the html code, it will render stuff, simple, efficient.

Bellow a simple html code to display an image and to constraint its width to 100px.

[code language="html"][/code]

src can be the local path to the image or its url. Let's see what IPython.core.display.HTML can do for us

[code language="python"]from IPython.core.display import HTML HTML('')[/code]

Having worked on some websites, I personally find it very satisfying to display an image with html code, that stuff is very smooth. The best part of this thing is yet to come :) . For now, let's write a simple fonction that automatically does the html formatting.

[code language="python"]def image_formatter_html(path_or_url): """html formatter for images. It takes as input an image path or a image url.""" html_code = f'< img src="{path_or_url}" width="100">' return html_code # Now we can do all the stuff with a one-liner. HTML(image_formatter_html(path_to_img))[/code]



DataFrame as a html table

Let's build a simple 3 columns DataFrame. One of the columns is logo_path and it contains the paths to the images

[code language="python"]import pandas as pd data_as_dict ={ "image_name":[ "logo_black", "logo_blue", "logo_double", "logo_purple" ], "image_description":[ "standard logo", "background blue", "double effect", "background purple" ], "logo_path":[ "images/standard_scaler_logo_black.jpg", "images/standard_scaler_logo_blue.jpg", "images/standard_scaler_logo_double.jpg", "images/standard_scaler_logo_purple.jpg" ] } df = pd.DataFrame(data_as_dict) df.head()[/code]

A nice feature in the pandas dataframe is that you can export it in html format with the command df.to_html() Another very cool stuff is that you can provide formatters to the to_html function. In other words we can use our previous function image_formatter_html to transform the column logo_path. For example images/standard_scaler_logo_black.jpg will become <img src="images/standard_scaler_logo_black.jpg" width=150>

[code language="python"]# Don't forget to set the `escape = False` argument otherwise # that won't work. The formatters argument takes a dictionary as input # it must have the following format {"column_name": formatting_function} html_code = df.to_html(formatters={'logo_path': image_formatter_html}, escape = False) HTML(html_code)[/code]

Isn't it beautiful ? :) . It will always amaze me how it can get me so excited to implement such basic stuff when we live in a world where super impressive things like ChatGPT exist :D

That being said, let's write the function that puts all the things together.

[code language="python"]def render_images_inside_df(df, path_column): """render images inside a dataframe by providing the column where we can find paths or urls to the images""" html_code = df.to_html(formatters={path_column: image_formatter_html}, escape = False) return HTML(html_code)[/code]
[code language="python"]render_images_inside_df(df, path_column='logo_path')[/code]

You can leave it as is if it suits you. If you want to refine a little more the function I can suggest you some more stuff. For instance we can add the img_width argument so that we can set the size of the images.

[code language="python"]def render_images_inside_df(df, path_column, img_width=150): """render images inside a dataframe by providing the column where we can find paths or urls to the images""" def image_formatter_html(path_or_url): """html formatter for images. It takes as input an image path or a image url.""" html_code = f'< img src="{path_or_url}" width="{img_width}">' return html_code return HTML(df.to_html(formatters={'logo_path': image_formatter_html}, escape = False))[/code]

Note that there is some sophistication here, we define an inner function image_formatter_html. Why is that so ? Recall that formatters takes a dictionary as input, it has to be in following format {"column_name": formatting_func} The thing is we can't pass any extra argument to formating_func. To address this problem we define an inner function so that we can have access to img_width without explicitly setting an extra argument to image_formatter_html.

[code language="python"]render_images_inside_df(df, path_column='logo_path', img_width=50)[/code]



Full code

[code language="python"]from IPython.core.display import HTML import pandas as pd def render_images_inside_df(df, path_column, img_width=150): """render images inside a dataframe by providing the column where we can find paths or urls to the images""" def image_formatter_html(path_or_url): """html formatter for images. It takes as input an image path or a image url.""" html_code = f'' return html_code return HTML(df.to_html(formatters={'logo_path': image_formatter_html}, escape = False))[/code]



Bonus - how to include the rendering function directly in the dataframe object by subclassing pd.DataFrame

If you are not familiar with the concept of classes in python, I recommend you to read on the subject before diving into this last paragraph. However if you are in a hurry or lazy, in a nutshell a class is a code template for creating objects. Objects have member variables and have behavior associated with them.

The idea here is to subclass pd.DataFrame and to add a function named render_images so that we can invoke it simply with a nasty df.render_images(...)

[code language="python"]import pandas as pd # Subclassing pd.DataFrame. In other words we create a new class "dataframe_plus" that is going to inherit # every existing functions of pd.DataFrame, we then add our own custom function class dataframe_plus(pd.DataFrame): def render_images(self, path_column, img_width=80): return render_images_inside_df(self, path_column, img_width)[/code]
[code language="python"]# Instantiate the dataframe with the brand new class "dataframe_plus" # We use the same data `data_as_dict` as used in the beginning of the post. df = dataframe_plus(data_as_dict)[/code]
[code language="python"]# Now we can call the function directly within the object, how cool is that ? df.render_images('logo_path')[/code]

Full code

In other words we create a new class "dataframe_plus" that is going to inherit # every existing functions of pd.DataFrame, we then add our own custom function class dataframe_plus(pd.DataFrame): def render_images(self, path_column, img_width=80): """render images inside a dataframe by providing the column where we can find paths or urls to the images""" def image_formatter_html(path_or_url): """html formatter for images. It takes as input an image path or a image url.""" html_code = f'' return html_code return HTML(self.to_html(formatters={'logo_path': image_formatter_html}, escape = False)) df = dataframe_plus(data_as_dict) df.render_images('logo_path')[/code]
