item.title: Mutual information simply explained with example and code - A generalization of the correlation concept.
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Mutual information is a very nice statistical tool that can be seen as a generalization of the correlation concept. Indeed, the pearson's correlation allows us to find out if two variables are linearly dependent. The thing is we are not always interested only in linear relationships, that's where mutual information comes into action. It can emphasize any kind of dependance between two distributions. Another cool thing about mutual information is that it can be used for both continuous and discrete variables.

The formula

The formula looks like this:

I've found out that many people struggle understanding what it exactly does, not because it's difficult to understand per se, but because they get confused by the notation and sometimes they also have some misconceptions. So let's dive into the subject step by step.

Notation and misconceptions

The core thing to understand is the concept of independence between two events A and B. The most intuitive way to understand it is perhaps to use conditional probabilities: Recall that P(A|B) (Probability of A given B) can be written like so:

if A and B are independents it means that knowing B doesn't help you predict A, in other words, it doesn't give you any information about A.

Thus the probability of A given B is simply the probability of A.
This leads to P(A and B) = P(A).P(B)

In other words, the product of the separate probabilities is equal to the probability that both events will occur.

I want to point out that most often the concept of independence is confused with the concept of mutuallly exclusive events. That is not the same thing !

Two events are mutually exclusive if they can not occur at the same time. For instance, a tossed coin outcome can be either heads or tails, but both outcomes cannot occur simultaneously, they are mutually exclusive.

On the other hand, two independent events do occur simultaneously, simply the probability of the intersection is exactly equal to the probability that both events occur.

One last thing that might disturb you is the notation p(A,B). This is exactly the same thing as P(A and B) or P(A ∩ B).
Moreover, there is a little bit of lingo to know here:

  • P(A, B) or P(A and B) or P(A ∩ B) is said to be the joint probability
  • P(A) is said to be the marginal probability
  • P(B) is said to be the marginal probability
  • P(A | B) is said to be the conditional probability

That's it ! A probability can be either marginal, joint or conditional.

Now that you are more familiar with the key concepts, the notation and the lingo we are ready to move forward.

A simple example

I've made up a dataset which features or columns are likes chocolate and gender. There are in fact 100 lines but I won't display the whole table for obvious reasons. :D

The random variable likes_chocolate has two possible events:

  • Yes
  • No

The random variable gender has two possible events:

  • Male
  • Female

From that, the idea is to see if gender affects likes_chocolate or not and vice versa. To do so we are going to change the granularity of the study and see if the events of gender do affect the events of likes_chocolate.

A simple idea is to build up a contingency table. This is a fancy word to call a table where you count the amount of occurrences of simultaneous events. If you prefere we can also say that this is a table showing the distribution of one variable in rows and another in columns. We use this to study the correlation between the two variables. For instance the first cell which value is 23 corresponds to the number of occurrences of the simultaneous events likes_chocolate = no and gender = female.

I have generated the data so that for each outcome female and male have 50% chance each to be drawn. In the same fashion, a person has 50% chance to like or not to like chocolate. In fact I've generated the data so that the variables are independent.

If the variables are perfectly independents, there is a priori no reason for a cell of the table to have more occurrences than another. We can also say that for given variables, in our case likes_chocolate and gender, if these two are independent, then there's no reason that gender affects likes_chocolate. In particular, there's no reason to observe a higher probability for the joint events gender=male and likes_chocolate = yes than for the joint events gender=female and likes_chocolate = yes. This holds true for all the other joint events (for every cell of the table).

What is interesting to understand here is that because the variables should be independent, one would expect to end end up with approximately 25 occurrences for each joint events.

That is actually what we see, although this is not exactly 25 occurences for each cell !

This is a toy example and frankly, we can already see that the variables are independent. However, "in the real life" everything is not perfectly balanced, so to ensure that the values of the cells remain comparable we use the following property of independence that we already spoke about:

The idea is simple. If A and B are independent then P(A and B) divided by P(A).P(B) is equal to one. Otherwise, if the ratio is way higher or way lesser than one then there is some dependency. So we are going to calculate how dependent are each pairs of events.

So first let's calculate all the pairs of P(A,B). The probability of A and B is simply the number of times events A and B occur simultaneously over the total number of possible outcomes (N). here N is 100 (this is the number of lines of the dataset). As we have a contingency table, we already have the occurrences of the pairs of events, we then simply need to divide all the values by 100.

Notice that we also added a total for the lines and columns. This is helpful as we will need to calculate the marginal probabilities P(female), P(male), P(likes_chocolate) and P(dont_like_chocolate). We can easily read for example that P(female)= 0.49.

Now the last step is to divide all the joint probabilities by the product of their marginal probabilities.

So we get a table where all the values are approximately equal to 1 meaning that all the pairs of events are independents (as expected).

Now if we were to flatten all the values of the table to make the array [0.94, 1.06, 1.06, 0.94] and display it as a bar plot, this would look like this.

I put "distribution" in quotation marks because usually what is meant by distribution is the probability distribution which values are supposed to add up to 1. Here we just see how the values are distributed but they are not proabilities.

This is interesting to stop a moment to think of what the problem has really become.

  • If you think about that, when all the events are independents, all the values are equal to 1 so the "distribution" is flat, consequently there is no clear pattern, we can also say that events are drawn from a uniform distribution and therefore the uncertainty is maximum.

  • When the variables are very dependents, we should see some values way higher than 1 and some way lesser than 1 (because for example if a pair of events occur 80 times then there is only 20 occurrences remaining for other events) So we are favoring pairs of events over others, in other words, we are reducing uncertainty.

So this is really becoming a problem of quantifying uncertainty in the distribution. This should be somewhat reminiscent of the concept of entropy. Please read my article about entropy if you are not familiar with this concept

From there, we just calculate the entropy of the "distribution". Entropy has this general form :

The only difference is really what's inside the log. Indeed, instead of having a probability inside, we'll have the previous quantity p(x,y)/p(x).p(y).

the log of p(x,y)/p(x).p(y) in our case has a name, it is called the pointwise mutual information or PMI.

The last step is to calculate the PMI of every possible x and y weighted by the probability p(x,y) that x and y occur together. This weighted average measures how much we expect the variables to be dependent of each other. We can also say that this measures how much we expect the variables to predict each other.

This leads us to the formula.

Or we can also write this in a more explicit way

Applied to our example, and with the help of our previous tables the calculation is as follows:

I(X, Y) = 0.23*log(0.94) + 0.27*log(1.06) + 0.26*log(1.06) + 0.24*log(0.94)
I(X, Y) ≈ 0

  • The mutual information is almost equal to 0 which means that the variables X=likes_chocolate and Y=gender don't share any information together, that is they are independent.

  • A usueful property to know is that the mutual information can never be lesser than 0.

  • When the mutual information is greater than 0 we can say that there is some dependency. The more the value is high the more there is dependency between variables. Unlike pearson's correlation, the upper bound of the mutual information is not 1. In fact there is an upper bound but it depends on your data. Usually it doesn't matter to know the upper bound as you just need a relative value so that you can sort all the features X_i that are the most correlated with a feature Y for instance. By the way, I'll show you how you could use mutual information as a feature selector in a bit :)

Mutual Information with continuous variables

Normally we can only use categorical variables with mutual information. The trick here is to transform continuous variables into categorial variables.

One way to do this is to use binning, which involves dividing the range of values of a continuous variable into a set of bins or intervals and assigning each observation to its corresponding bin.

Here a simple example with bins=2 and bins=3. The number of bins is the number of categories you want to build up. In the example, we have a continuous variable lkes_chocolate_score that we are going to discretize or to transform into categories.

Use mutual information as a way to do feature selection

You can use the following code to test de dependency of several features of X against the target variable Y

[code language="python"]from sklearn.datasets import load_iris from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif # Load the iris dataset iris = load_iris() # Separate the features (X) from the target (y) X = iris.data y = iris.target # Compute the mutual information between each feature and the target mutual_info = mutual_info_classif(X, y) # Print the mutual information scores for each feature for i in range(len(mutual_info)): print(f"{iris.feature_names[i]}: {mutual_info[i]:.3f}")[/code] 
sepal length (cm): 0.488
sepal width (cm): 0.258
petal length (cm): 0.985
petal width (cm): 0.969

In this example, we first load the iris dataset from the sklearn.datasets module. We then separate the features (X) from the target (y).

Next, we use the mutual_info_classif function to compute the mutual information between each feature and the target. It returns an array of mutual information scores, one for each feature.

Finally, we print out the mutual information score for each feature using a loop. The output will show the mutual information score for each of the four features in the iris dataset.

To select features based on mutual information, we have to choose the features with the highest scores. These features are considered to have the strongest relationship with the target variable and are likely to provide the most valuable information for predicting the target. In our example petal_width and petal_length appear to be the features that are highly related to the target variable.

That's it for today, thank you for reading !

item.title: What are Data Drift and Concept Drift in Machine Learning ? MLOps Simply explained.
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Once you have trained a successful machine learning model that meets the standards you want to achieve, you can celebrate it ! However, this is far from beeing the end of the story. In fact, most of the time it's the easiest part :D . Now, you have to make the model available at scale for users as an app. This step is called deployment.

Like any normal app, machine learning models may encounter bugs over time, so you occasionally have to change the code in order to fix them. By the way, as you changed the code, what you fixed might have changed the behaviour of other functions. You then have to make sure all the functions still behave the same way. This step is usually performed through unit testing and integration testing. Finally, you have to redeploy the whole app.

In addition, users may also request new features to enhance the app, so again you'll need to change the code, perform tests and redeploy it.

In a nutshell, there is an endless cycle: development, testing, deployment, monitoring, development, testing....

I think you can guess how annoying it would be to redo all these steps by hand each time. You need to automate this process! The process of maintaing your app throughout the software development life cycle in such a fashion is called DevOps.

In machine learning, we have MLOps it sounds like DevOps but there's a difference. We have all the previous things to take care of... but we also have other sources of hassle. Indeed, the performances of your model can degrade over time. Typically, Data Drift and Concept Drift are common causes of performance degradation in machine learning models.

In this article, we will focus on the later two.

Monitoring the performances

To illustrate the point, let's consider a simple example of a machine learning model that measures the willingness to buy an Iphone given the age. Your model has a very good accuracy for now, however, as you are a fellow MLOps Engineer, you want to keep an eye on the metrics over time. In order to evaluate the performance of the model, you need to calculate the error between its predictions and the true values. Wait a second, How do we calculate the error if we don't have access to the true values at the time of prediction ? In many real use cases you can have access to the true values with a delay. In our example, let's assume that a month after the predictions, you know if the people have indeed bought the phone or not so you can record the predictions in logs and calculate the error later when the outcomes become available.

In January, your model achieved high accuracy.

In February your model's accuracy is very low.

What happened ? Is that even possible ? Does it come from the model ? Is it the Data ? We need to investigate the possible causes of this discrepancy.

To begin the investigation, let's examine the model.

The blue line in this graph represents the predictions made by the model we trained. The red line shows the actual values that we are trying to predict.

The model appears to accurately predict most of the values of the target variable. A priori, it seems that the model is performing well overall.

Data Drift

Let's now take a closer look at the Data in january.

It seems to follow a bell curve or a normal/gaussian distribution in the statistics lingo. The majority of individuals fall between the ages of 20 and 40. As you can see from the blue line on the previous graph, the model's predictions for these age ranges are almost perfectly accurate. The rest of the ages are under-represented. As a result, the model's overall average error is very low.

Now let's look at the Data in February

This is kind of extreme, but let's assume this is not a bug and that it reflects real market behavior.

Now, the model is still the same, but all the data we have has shifted towards the 50-60 years old age range. As a consequence, the model is performing very poorly because all the data is located in the area where the model has the highest error.

So overall, the average error is very high.

This is what we call a Data Drift

Again, my example is quite extreme, in general your distribution is just a little bit skewed but we can clearly see the impact that the distribution can have on the model.

How to detect Data Drift ?

In fact, when monitoring for Data Drift, we don't even need to use the predictions or the real values. We only need to check that the new data is approximately distributed like the original one. A simple thing to implement, for example, is to set an alert when the mean/median of the data becomes too different from the mean of the original data. Generally speaking, we should monitor statistical properties of the input data, such as the mean, standard deviation, and correlation coefficients. Of course, we can use more advanced tools like statistical tests, etc.

A Data Drift almost always harms your model's performance, and it should always raise attention as it can potentially cause significant problems for the model's accuracy and reliability.

How to address Data Drift ?

There are several things you can do:

  • In our example we can retrain the model with the initial Dataset on which we'll add more data in the area where the model performs poorly (between 50 and 60) it could solve the problem.
  • If the Data Drift is small, fine-tuning the model may be sufficient.
  • If the data drift is significant, you may need to retrain the model on new data.

Concept Drift

Suppose it is September, and the model has been performing well until November.

However, in December, the model's performance has dropped significantly, even though the distribution of the data remains constant. So, what could be the reason behind this sudden drop in performance ?

Okay, now that should be the model's fault, right ?

Let's see what happened.

Oh my god, this time the model has literally flipped. Meaning that the true relationship between X and the target variable has completly changed while your model has remained the same. If we think about that, Apple launches a new Iphone every september so the previous iPhone may become less desirable for people between the ages of 20 and 40, leading to a significant shift in the target variable. However, younger and older people may not be as influenced by the trend, and may still be willing to buy the product, resulting in a complete change in the target variable distribution.

In essence, Concept drift is a phenomenon that occurs when the statistical properties of the target variable (the thing the model is trying to predict) change over time, rendering the model less accurate or even completely obsolete. This can occur due to changes in the behavior of the system being modeled, changes in the external environment, or other factors...

How to detect Concept Drift ?

Well, you need to analyze your model's performance over time and compare it to its performance on historical data. If the distribution of the target variable remains relatively stable but your model's performance deteriorates, it may indicate a Concept Drift. If you don't have access to the true values to calculate the error, you can consider maintaining a static model as a baseline for comparison.

For classification models, you can also check the average confidence score. If it changes significantly over time, it could be an indication of Concept Drift and should be investigated further.

How to address Concept Drift ?

When there is a Concept Drift in the data, it is usually necessary to retrain the model on new data to update the model and ensure that it remains accurate and reliable. This implies collecting new data that reflects the new distribution or behavior of the system.

Moreover, we may also have to change the model architecture or create a new one. For example, if the true relationship between X and Y changes from linear to logarithmic, we not only have to gather new data but also adapt the model.

A good practice is to regularly retrain and update the model to ensure that it remains accurate and reliable over time.

Other things you should be Monitoring:

In addition to model performance, drifts, and bugs, there are several other factors that you should consider.

  • Outliers: Identify and handle outliers in the input data, as these can skew the model's output and lead to inaccurate predictions (this can be part of the Data Drift monitoring).

  • Bias: Monitor for bias in the model's output, especially when the model is used in sensitive applications. Ensure that the model does not discriminate against certain groups of people and that its predictions are fair and ethical.

  • Robustness: Test the model's robustness by introducing adversarial examples or other forms of attacks that could potentially fool the model. This can help you identify and fix vulnerabilities in the model before they are exploited.

That's all for today folks, I hope you enjoyed this article !

item.title: The Data Scientist made ChatGPT and ChatGPT undid the Data Scientist.
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
(This article is a transcript in English of one of my french LinkedIn posts)

The headline is deliberately provocative... Nevertheless, I observe that in recent years many jobs in Data have begun a "metamorphosis". Among them, the job of Data Scientist is undoubtedly the one that has changed the most.

Just a few years ago, a Data Scientist could, with his PC and Jupyter Notebook "contribute to science" with his knowledge of math, statistics and motivation! His main job was to design machine learning models and train them. If we want to simplify, we can say he was an "R&D Data Scientist".

Gradually, there was a shift from the "classic" DS because with the arrival of increasingly efficient and accessible machine learning tools and libraries, designing models became an increasingly uncomplicated task. On the other hand, industrializing models and monitoring their life cycle became critical issues. This led to the emergence of the ML Engineer and MLOps Engineer.

Their jobs were now to design systems and maintain them over time.

At the same time, the job of Data Scientist became more specialized, it is increasingly difficult to be competent in both tabular data processing, NLP and Computer Vision. Some Data Scientists therefore now focus on a domain of expertise.

Then, with the emergence of very large models such as LLMs, designing state-of-the-art models is becoming, in part, a luxury reserved for companies that have very large computing capabilities and a lot of money! Not just anyone can work on a daily basis designing and training models like GPT3.5 or GPT4.

So the DS job is changing again, it's less and less about training new models from scratch, but more about using pre-trained models, adjusting them, and assembling them to form a coherent system. In other words, the S in Data Scientist is starting to falter as the job shifts little by little towards Engineering. In fact, we should talk more about AI Engineer.

Today, some of the DS's prerogatives are still nibbled a little more by Generative AI by automating certain data collection, cleaning, labeling and code generation tasks.

Data Scientist is becoming a very (too) generic term that can refer to both the R&D DS, the ML Engineer, the MLOps Engineer and the AI Engineer (and sometimes even the Data Engineer).

The Data Scientist still retains all his relevance and expertise, even if his scope has shifted with technological developments. His role is not called into question but is transforming enormously.

Finally, what is a Data Scientist in 2023?

item.title: The importance of monitoring LLMs performances in production
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Is ChatGPT becoming less capable over time?

(This article is a transcript in English of one of my french LinkedIn posts)

This is what a recent Stanford study suggests, which caused quite a stir over the past few days:

While the study is debated, it raises a very interesting point.

The need to have a system to evaluate the performance of LLMs (Large Language Models) in production.

Whether you use different models via an API, compare open source models, or explore fine-tuned versions of the same model, you will need a point of comparison.

The authors proceeded as follows:

They created sets of questions covering 4 tasks: solving math problems, answering sensitive questions, generating functional code, and formulating visual reasoning.

What is interesting is that one reason for choosing these types of problems is that they have objective answers and are therefore easy to evaluate. Another noteworthy point is that through the ability to answer sensitive questions, they quantified the model's propensity to give answers it should not (crucial for evaluating its ethics).

Regarding the metrics used:

  • Accuracy (rate of correct answers or executable code portion depending on the task)
  • Verbosity (length of response)
  • Overlap of responses between two versions of the same model

Measuring overlap may seem surprising at first, but it is also interesting! It allows quantifying to what extent two versions of the same model (here GPT-3.5 in March and June 2023) give the same response to the same question. In other words, it measures the "continuity" between two versions. I think we could, for example, reuse this approach to compare two differently fine-tuned versions of the same model.

Finally, they concluded that between two versions of GPT-4, performance significantly declined.

In any case, I think there are quite a few interesting ideas to leverage...

In case you woudlike to reuse the datasets of questions used in the paper, here is the link to the project: https://github.com/lchen001/LLMDrift

item.title: Should we redefine our conception of intelligence ?
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
(This article is a transcript in English of one of my french LinkedIn posts)

We will undoubtedly have to redefine our conception of intelligence.

With the emergence of all the new artificial intelligence models, and especially LLMs, I think we will have to collectively find a new way to define what we call "intelligence" and how we measure it.

Indeed, a model like GPT-4 that scores between 125 and 155 on an IQ test raises questions. This is troubling because we know that LLMs do not really have intelligence as we conceive it in humans, they do not have conscious intelligence. We can therefore question the aspects of intelligence that are really measured by these tests.

Similarly, I would like to make a small parallel in education: the fact that ChatGPT passes bar exams or business school exams leads to thinking about selection criteria (if we want selection criteria based on "intelligence"). Maybe in the future we will have to favor human-to-human interactions and real-life situations, rather than paper exams?

On the other hand, should we try to endow AI with some form of consciousness so that they are really intelligent?

All these questions are exciting and I really look forward to seeing what the future holds.

Finally, I looked at a lot of definitions and quotes about intelligence, asking myself each time "Could this apply to ChatGPT?" Often the answer was "Yes..." But one quote stood out because it opens up stimulating avenues for thought and remains relevant today:

"Intelligence is not what you know but what you do when you don't know." - Jean Piaget (psychologist, 1896-1980)

item.title: Are you ready for the Machine Unlearning challenge ?
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
(This article is a transcript in English of one of my french LinkedIn posts)

Have you heard about the Machine Unlearning challenge?

It's an ethics-oriented challenge, launched by researchers from Google DeepMind. The challenge consists of making the model forget part of its training data. In other words, it involves removing the influence of a subset of the training data from the weights of an already trained model.

Machine unlearning is currently a very active area of research because the question of ethics arises more and more, and it raises new technical challenges with it.

Indeed, when you train a model with a dataset, the learning materializes from the model's point of view by changing its weights. The problem is that if tomorrow you are asked to make the model forget some data (under the right to be forgotten in particular), it's very complicated. There is no obvious mapping between the training data and its materialization as weights.

In addition, there is an issue with maintaining satisfactory performance in production after "forgetting the data", because performance will inevitably be impacted.

You have to find the best compromise between effective forgetting and preserving the model's performance.

For the challenge, you have at your disposal an image classification model (ResNet18) and the CIFAR10 dataset.

You will have to submit an algorithm that takes 3 inputs:

  • The ResNet18 model pre-trained on the entire initial dataset
  • The set of images to forget "forget"
  • The set of images to retain "retain" and outputs:

An updated ResNet18 model that has "forgotten" the data from the "forget" set.

How is this evaluated?

Submissions are evaluated using:

Tools similar to MIA - (Membership Inference Attack) Statistical tests to quantify the difference between the distribution of the "unlearned" model and the original model. To help you, there is a starter kit with a notebook that goes into detail on the objectives. As an example and for inspiration, the notebook also proposes a simple but suboptimal solution, which consists of fine-tuning the model on the "retain set" for 5 epochs, which has the consequence of sufficiently affecting the weights to blur the "forget set".

Challenge link

item.title: Unmasking Confidential Data in ML Models with Membership Inference Attacks
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
(This article is a transcript in English of one of my french LinkedIn posts)

MIA, or Membership Inference Attack, is a technique that lets you determine whether specific data was used to train a ML model. It can be used for malicious purposes or, on the contrary, to audit cybersecurity.

In particular, when auditing a model, MIA can be used to check if confidential data was unknowingly used by the model.

The major challenge is that when you test an online AI service, you don't have access to the model's internal architecture or how it was trained. You're faced with a "black box": you feed it data and get back predictions, without knowing what's happening inside.

But how do we proceed?

ML models learn from a training dataset. Meanwhile, Data Scientists must ensure that these models don't overfit and can generalize to new data. A strong assumption used by MIA is that, despite precautions, these models still tend to be more confident about data they've seen during training.

For instance, for an image classification into 3 categories, if prediction probabilities are [99%, 0.5%, 0.5%], one could argue the model is "unusually" certain. Hence, it's likely that the image was part of the training data.

However, at this stage, we generally don't have access to these probabilities. So, we need to find a technique to indirectly estimate them.

To do this, we'll create our own models. Either we manage to gather information on the target architecture, or we "guess" it or at least create models with similar behavior. These exact or approximate clones are called "shadow models."

Now, we need data to train these shadow models. This is probably the most complex part since you either need access to data similar to the target model's or you must generate a synthetic dataset by iterating on the target model using specific techniques.

Lastly, we need another model known as the "attack" model. This takes the probabilities from the shadow model and will determine if the data was part of the target model's training set or not.

There are some reservations: It's a relatively complex method with limited applicability. It's primarily effective on modest-sized models, supervised learning, or GANs. Moreover, recent criticisms of MIA suggest their efficiency largely depends on models' overfitting.

It's safe to say that they can't really be applied to LLMs right now.

But in the near future, who knows?"

item.title: Does no one care about Data Drift in LLMOps ?
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
(This article is a transcript in English of one of my french LinkedIn posts)

By the way, there is indeed a term to describe the life cycle management of language models: LLMOps (In the Ops family, following Dev and ML, meet the newest member, LLMOps).

But back to our question: I had this thought: why doesn't Data Drift seem to concern many when using LLMs? By Data Drift, I mean the evolution of input data (the prompts) over time, which could impact the model's performance. I searched scientific publications, blogs, content specialized in LLMOps... Not much to find.

It simply doesn't seem to be a topic.

Is it because this emerging discipline still lacks maturity and tools to tackle this issue? Admittedly, "classic" MLOps hasn't reached its full maturity either.

Or is it because LLMs are trained on such massive amounts of data that the risk of drift between production and training data is minimal? Therefore, it wouldn't affect the model's performance?

Or, is it because the input data (the prompts) are shaped and reshaped by the user until the desired result is obtained? So the drift of the prompts wouldn't be an issue.

However, even if we assume that drift doesn't affect LLMs much (which is debatable), monitoring it seems crucial in many cases...

Suppose users find a flaw in your production LLM, spread the word, and overnight, hundreds of them have fun generating malicious code with your service.

Without data drift monitoring, how can you detect that something is happening?

But then again, how to measure it effectively?

I guess one solution would be to regularly collect a representative sample of embeddings associated with user prompts, and then devise a clustering and divergence measurement solution based on that.

Assuming this works and is scalable, there are still data privacy concerns.

If you store the embeddings of the prompts, it means that you could, using certain techniques, roughly reconstruct the original prompts (though it's not that straightforward)…

I have so many questions!

In short, data drift with LLMs seems to be a blind spot even though its monitoring seems crucial to me. Between the lack of maturity of tools, the massive amount of training data, and user intervention on input data, several hypotheses might explain this "lack of interest."

I am very curious to hear your thoughts on this!

I'm also looking for resources on the topic

item.title: From Data Scientist to Data Engineer... ultimately to AI Engineer.
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
(This article is a transcript in English of one of my french LinkedIn posts)

Lately, a clear trend of many Data Scientists moving towards Data Engineer roles has been observed.

This phenomenon can be attributed to several factors:

First and foremost, the job market is undergoing significant changes, and Data Engineers capable of building robust and scalable data pipelines are in high demand. Consequently, it is currently easier to find positions as a Data Engineer than a Data Scientist. Notably, Data Scientists (and ML Engineers for that matter) often possess knowledge in cloud, Python, and tools like Docker, GitLab, or Terraform, which facilitates a transition to the Data Engineer profession (requiring a varying degree of effort).

No doubt, some Data Scientists are frustrated by spending considerable time on "data wrangling" (data cleaning and preparation). Moreover, certain Data Scientists might feel weariness after dedicating much time to develop POCs (proof of concept) that don't yield tangible outcomes. On the contrary, some might feel stagnant working on the same use-cases for extended periods. By transitioning to a Data Engineer role, they can rejuvenate their experience by focusing on building sturdy data infrastructures and gaining solid technical skills.

Other Data Scientists, who were torn between software engineering and the mathematical/statistical aspect, find that they are more inclined towards the software side.

To top it all, the DS to DE transition can often take place within the same company.

More recently, a new trend is emerging with the rise of LLMs (Large Language Models). Indeed, these models become accessible through simple API calls, greatly reducing the entry barrier to the world of AI and ML. Subsequently, one can develop comprehensive applications focusing mainly on the software development aspect. Hence, an increasing number of software engineers are getting involved in building AI solutions.

It's fascinating to observe the overlaps emerging between the various data professions, and this might just be the beginning…

With the current enthusiasm and the "sexy" allure of generative models, combined with the need for ever-more sophisticated architectures to deploy open-source LLMs like Llama-2 in the cloud, might we see a reverse trend? Perhaps, witnessing Data Engineers transitioning to AI Engineer roles?

item.title: Conveying complex ideas intuitively is an art
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
(This article is a transcript in English of one of my french linkedIn posts)

Conveying complex ideas intuitively is an art. As Andrew Ng says "Before diving into the subject, I first want to give you the intuition." Most people in AI have at some point taken one of his courses, and his teaching style leaves no one indifferent! More broadly, I admire personalities like Andrew Ng, Luis Serrano, Jay Alammar - they know, in my opinion, how to convey complex concepts intuitively. This is a skill I have often lacked in my own journey.

Indeed, I remember many classes, especially in mathematics, where priority was given to rigorous proof rather than developing intuition. Once the proof was presented, the teacher often considered the subject closed and understood by all. On the contrary, I have often had physics teachers whose main goal was to "explain with their hands" without proving anything. After all, this story of "intuiting" a concept must be, somehow, a physicist thing.

I am convinced that what really helps to durably assimilate a concept is to start by giving an intuitive representation, a mental image. It is essential in my opinion to develop an instinctive understanding of the underlying mechanisms before diving into the proofs.

Of course, some rigorous proofs can be exciting and essential. But are they really useful for all students? Probably not. Especially when they are presented as a mandatory step, without any apparent connection to concrete reality.

That's the problem: theoretical proofs often do not advance intuitive understanding. They are then likely to discourage more than anything else those who struggle to connect them to their intuition.

On the other hand, I have always been fascinated by short, elegant proofs that open your eyes to an almost cheeky way to solve the problem. They are powerful because they require a bird's eye view, a real step back from the problem. They also reveal a certain beauty in mathematical reasoning. The famous proofs that start with "we notice that" and 2 lines later the matter is settled, while in parallel an alternative proof consists in deploying brute force and filling 3 full pages.

I think this ability to explain things simply is very undervalued. It also requires being able to relate to learners, which is not always easy! I also notice that there is often a premium on complexity nowadays. No doubt it is also more reassuring and gratifying for the teacher to show that he can do complex reasoning?

I am very curious to know your point of view on this issue! Does your experience match this observation?

item.title: Data Science Students: Forget the Models, Focus on Deployment
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
(This article is a transcript in English of one of my french linkedIn posts)

Recently, I started posting regularly on LinkedIn. As a result, many Data Science students have contacted me, seeking advice on landing an internship, apprenticeship, or first job. The resumes I've seen are often very interesting, but they all have one thing in common: they focus on theory and model understanding. Machine Learning, Deep Learning, using Transformers, Computer Vision models... all of this is great! But I've noticed there is often not much on the deployment side.

The reality is that many training programs don't include teaching how to put models into production. Yet today, the ability to deploy them and manage their life cycle (MLOps) is arguably a more sought-after skill by companies than mastery of the Data Scientist's "classic" toolbox.

If I have one piece of advice to give you: stand out by carrying out one or more projects focused on deployment. Develop web applications with Flask or FastAPI, get familiar with CI/CD, dive into infrastructure as code, and explore tools like SageMaker.

With a little resourcefulness you won't have to pay a cent using Amazon's Free Tier offering.

The aim of this tutorial is to learn GitHub Pages and enhance your skills in HTML, CSS and JavaScript by building a website in a fun, engaging way. We'll use ChatGPT to guide and enhance the learning process.

Let's start by designing a simple landing page for an AI company using GitHub Pages. This can later be expanded into a full website

Chek out the resulting website here
You can find the full Github example here

Prerequisites

  • A GitHub Account
  • Git command knowledge
  • Basic understanding of HTML and CSS.
  • [OPTIONAL] An IDE such as VScode, pycharm ...

As you know, I myself have a basic grasp of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript since it's not my regular focus, but ChatGPT has got your back

What is GitHub Pages ?

GitHub Pages is a GitHub service for hosting static websites directly from repositories.

It's free, user-friendly, supports custom domains, and integrates with Jekyll. Additionally, it leverages Git's version control.

However, it's limited to static content, has a 1GB repository size cap, and lacks advanced backend features like databases. So if you’re expecting a lot of traffic or want complex features, paying for a great hosting service would be the way to go.

Prohibited uses : GitHub Pages is not intended for or allowed to be used as a free web-hosting service to run your online business, e-commerce site, or any other website that is primarily directed at either facilitating commercial transactions or providing commercial software as a service (SaaS). GitHub Pages sites shouldn't be used for sensitive transactions like sending passwords or credit card numbers. See GitHub's documentation on prohibited uses for more details.

Setup the github project

I suppose that you are already familiar with the basics of github and git commands, if it's not the case, there are plenty of free resources on the net, please check them before diving into this tutorial.

Once you are logged in to your Github account, go to your repositories and create a new one

Note that in order to publish a GitHub Pages site, your repository must be public. Private repositories are not supported for hosting GitHub Pages websites for free

After the repository has been created, you can copy its link.

Now you can clone the project locally using either a terminal window or the built-in terminal in the IDE of your choice

[code language="bash"]git clone link-to-your-github-project.git cd your-github-project[/code]

ChatGPT to the rescue

Now we'll have ChatGPT do most of the work for us, the idea is to get him generate the components of our website, that is to say:

  • index.html:
    file that contains the structure and content of web pages using HTML markup. They define the semantic elements like headings, paragraphs, links, etc

  • style.css:
    file to add styling to web pages using CSS code. They control visual elements like colors, layout, fonts, etc.

  • script.js:
    file to add interactivity and dynamic behavior to web pages using JavaScript code. They enable functionality like click events, animations, data manipulation, etc.

To properly follow along with this tutorial, you can access the full chat history here

- index.html
index has to reference style.css and script.js

Remember it has to be very attractive ! Do not provide only raw html please.
You can resize the logo if you want.

Note that I added an image of the logo to my repository beforehand, so I was able to reference its link in the code ChatGPT generated, even though this may not be the best way to do it.

item.title: LinkedIn's AI "Experts"
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
(This article is a transcript in English of one of my french linkedIn posts)

AI experts are sprouting up on LinkedIn even as it becomes increasingly difficult to actually be one.

It's becoming harder to call oneself an expert because data roles are evolving into "super roles". They require more and more varied skills, and with innovation cycles becoming shorter, near-constant awareness is needed.

Take the Data Scientist - they increasingly need to develop ML Engineering and MLOps skills, while the Data Engineer is becoming more of what we call a Platform Engineer (also known as SRE or even Cloud Engineer). The sought-after profiles are increasingly well-rounded and the technologies increasingly numerous.

At the same time, we see many people on LinkedIn with no theoretical AI knowledge presenting themselves as "experts". These are often newcomers to the field who have learned to master consumer tools and become "super techies". While not questioning their self-taught skills, sometimes brilliantly executed, it seems risky to self-proclaim as an expert (because clearly they aren't) without a solid technical background.

On further reflection, I believe the majority are acting in good faith but simply do not realize "the extent of their ignorance".

Indeed, paradoxically it's often those who know the least who overestimate their knowledge. We can all remember a high school friend who after an exam thought they aced it only to be baffled by a 4/20 score. They simply lacked the minimal skills to gauge their true level.

There's a term for this cognitive bias – the Dunning-Kruger effect. Étienne Klein likes to talk about Ultracrepidarianism.

According to Dunning and Kruger there are 3 phases in learning:

1/ Mount Stupid: you start in the field and quickly believe you're an ace.

2/ Valley of Humility: you realize the extent of your missing knowledge and tend towards imposter syndrome.

3/ Plateau of Consolidation: you develop a realistic assessment of your own skills.

The original 1999 Dunning-Kruger study has also had its share of criticism over time but I believe it still reflects a certain reality that can be verified in data.

As a result, I feel the term "expert" has been devalued. Today, when I see "AI Expert" instead of being reassured, I'm apprehensive from the outset.

In the end, this Confucius quote perfectly sums up this post: "True knowledge is knowing the extent of one's ignorance".

Do you know the extent of your ignorance? When do you think one can call themselves an expert? What does an expert look like versus a senior?

item.title: The future of generative AI will likely not be made of ever-larger models
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
(This article is a transcript in English of one of my french linkedIn posts)

The future of generative AI will likely not be made of ever-larger models.

In recent years, the dominant impression was that the only way to improve language model performance was to increase their number of parameters. This frantic "scale" race seems unsustainable in the long run.

Sam Altman himself stated last April: "Future progress won't simply come from bigger models." We have probably reached the end of the era of gigantic models.

There are several arguments that lead me to say we're entering an inflection point:

▶ We will hit two types of limits: costs and available data.
▶ There is currently a GPU shortage that prompts rethinking approaches.
▶ It does not align with history for cutting-edge AI to be the exclusive domain of a handful of players.
▶ Most current models are still highly suboptimal.

It is this last point I want to dig into here.

Recent work like Google DeepMind's "Chinchilla" research paper published in March 2022 shows many models are under-trained - meaning training them longer on more data could improve performance.

This also means smaller models trained on more data can reach the same performance level.

The "Chinchilla" researchers sought to determine the optimal parameter and data amounts for a given compute budget (FLOPS). They conducted a vast study training 400 models with variations in size, training time, and data volume ingested. One interesting paper result is it would take 20x more tokens than parameters for optimal results. Researchers built the "Chinchilla" model following this finding.

Chinchilla, with 70 billion parameters, outperforms GPT-3 which has 175 billion.

Chinchilla has fewer parameters but was trained on 1.4 trillion tokens, 20x the number of parameters, while GPT-3 was trained on 300 billion tokens, just 2x the parameters.

Meta's latest July Llama 2 model goes even further, with the 70B version trained on 2 trillion tokens - a ratio of 28.

Knowing this, there is an advantage to making smaller models, as they take up less storage space, require less GPU power for inference, are more easily deployable (and cheaper), and can be more accessible to the community.

I think in the future it won't stop there, we will certainly find even more optimized architectures. In my opinion, the future belongs to compact, efficient models.

It's only a matter of time before we can run highly capable LLM directly on our smartphones.

Sources:

  • Chinchilla paper
  • Sam Altman's claim

item.title: From Excel to Snowflake: Bridging the Data Culture Gap
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
(This article is a transcript in english of one of my french linkedin posts)

We must realize that we live in a world where companies still fully operate with Excel to store, analyze, and dashboard data, while on the other side, companies adopt a "modern data stack" with technologies like Snowflake, dbt, Tableau, and even LLM.

When one is immersed daily in a data environment, the Excel-centric approach can seem a bit obsolete. It's a somewhat "manual" approach prone to errors, without real data governance, and above all, difficult to scale.

Of course, it's far from the ideal solution, but if you think about it, it's an approach that can still work today in cases where the volume of available data is still low. In that case, it's mostly a matter of priority, of knowing how to focus on what really creates value for the company.

Because after all, why do we create all this data infrastructure, so complex, if not to create value?

And there too, there is an issue we need to discuss... The value created by these data platforms is not always noticeable by executives and decision makers.

We can't really blame them, because the crux of the problem is that to really perceive this value, you need a certain data culture that is not easy to acquire (the famous data acculturation).

At a minimum, to clarify the situation, one solution would be to design the data platform, from the start, as a product in its own right, define success metrics and track progress. On the other hand, use a business case driven approach to gradually grow the platform. Create value by starting small and then growing progressively.

These elements can help better understand what's going on and keep track.

Then, I also think it's our role, as data practitioners, to make this world more accessible to the "average joe". To show that data provides useful daily insights, that it structures the company, that it provides a competitive edge...

Finally, it may seem trivial, but one of the first barriers to understanding is already data jargon, which is not yet well defined by the way, differs from one company to another and can even cause comprehension problems between different data scientists or data engineers.

The data scientist, data engineer or data strategist roles themselves are still far from being well understood by the majority of people on this planet

item.title: The Fuzzy Notion of Overfitting with GPT4 - What Does it Mean to Overfit on All Knowledge?
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
What could it possibly mean to overfit on 'all available knowledge'? The notion of overfitting for GPT4 is fuzzy. Does it still make sense?

With the emergence of huge language models like GPT4, the classical notion of overfitting becomes abstract, at least for me.

In traditional machine learning, we try to prevent the model from overfitting the training data. We look for a good balance between overfitting and underfitting to maintain the model's ability to generalize, beyond the training set. In short, so it can adapt to new data.

With the advent of enormous language models like GPT4, what could it possibly mean to overfit on 'all available knowledge'?

In this case, isn't overfitting what we're looking for?

Assuming we have an infinite training budget, one could consider that we want GPT-4 to "overfit" as much as possible the extent of human knowledge. If GPT4 overfits, wouldn't that be a sign that it captures a large part of the subtleties and nuances of human language?

The term overfitting itself is probably not very suitable for very large LMs, because even if it sees "the same information" several times, it will be with different nuances.

On closer reflection, we probably don't want to overfit on all this knowledge because there is a good chance that the information present is not reliable in its entirety.

Of course, my thinking remains wishful, but I find that it illustrates well how very large language models push the boundaries of traditional concepts in machine learning.

item.title: Large Language Models Are Not One-Size-Fits-All for NLP
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Using a jackhammer to crack a nut... That's kind of what we're doing when we use a large language model for a basic NLP task... What about good old TF-IDF?

We've gotten into the habit of using large language models for all sorts of tasks. We have to admit, they've become easy to access via APIs, interfaces, cloud provider services or even locally. But this ease of use shouldn't lead to laziness, especially when it comes to being more efficient and less demanding on computing resources.

Let's consider the use case where we need to select keywords from a text. For example, to classify a document or to automatically suggest tags to a user for SEO.

There is a proven NLP method that allows us to do this fairly easily. It's called TF-IDF.

Suppose we have a corpus of documents. The statistical TF-IDF method assumes that important words are probably not the ones that are abundant across all documents, because those are common.

On the flip side, words that are frequent in only a few documents are likely the most important.

For a given word, in a given document, the score assigned is:

The frequency of the word's appearance in the document (TF - Term Frequency).

Weighted by the ratio of the total number of documents over the number of documents where the term appears (IDF - Inverse Document Frequency).

I suggest a little code example on Github using the first paragraph of the iPhone Wikipedia page. I "cheat" a bit by using each sentence as a document, clean up the words a bit, do some lemmatization, and apply tf-idf using bigrams (consecutive word pairs) as well.

The result isn't perfect but this low-cost method can largely suffice in some cases. Plus, it can be refined later with more advanced techniques.

Of course tf-idf has its limitations, it's a purely statistical method and thus doesn't take semantics into account. It requires a certain number of documents and words for the result to be relevant, etc... But NLP shouldn't be reduced to just large language models!

item.title: The Era of Fast and Inexpensive LLM is Underway and Microsoft is Joining the Dance!
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
The Era of Fast and Inexpensive LLM is Underway and Microsoft is Joining the Dance!

This current trend of focusing on developing capable but smaller LMs is not displeasing to me because although recently unveiled models like Falcon 180B are impressive, I doubt many companies in France have use cases that would justify the cost of deploying and maintaining these models in the cloud (you need 8 40GB A100 GPUs just to load the model).

On the other hand, I am much more stimulated by a model like Microsoft's recently published 1.3B parameter Phi 1.3B because I think that today models between 1 and 13B parameters meet most of the needs of companies.

Today, the war is more than ever to reduce inference costs.

Until now, to make models more compact, we could turn to small LLM and use fine-tuning to specialize them on a specific task, thus avoiding the use of larger generalist models.

We can also use "quantization", i.e. reduce the model weight size by reducing the precision of the calculations (for example from 32 bits to 16, 8 or even 4...).

(There are other techniques like knowledge distillation or low rank factorization but they are a bit less accessible.)

Another lever we can act on is the neural network architecture.

Transformers that emerged in 2017 are still the basis for today's LLM.

The Transformer architecture has a small flaw: its inference complexity is linear with sequence length, i.e. O(N), due in particular to its characteristic attention layers.

Yesterday, Microsoft (again) published an article to suggest an alternative to Transformers: the "RetNet" and the results are promising! The inference complexity is constant, i.e. O(1). In particular, inference would be 8.4x faster than with Transformers while saving 70% of GPU memory.

To get concrete, today to load a 7B LLM on your GPU you need 14GB of memory (with 16-bit precision).

The longer the text sequence to process, the more additional GPU your model will consume, up to 45GB of RAM in the example.

With RetNet we stay constant around 15GB.

I'm excited and at the same time part of me invites me to remain cautious, others have already tried to replace Transformers, without success.

Wait and see!

item.title: Can AI-Generated Art be Considered Real Art?
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Can AI-Generated Art be Considered Real Art?

I was struck yesterday by the comments I found on a LinkedIn post (post in comments). The post in question highlighted a series of images generated by AI. This type of image is created using an image generation model like Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, DALL-E. But they also have the particularity of using an additional model called ControlNet which guides the first.

The problem with image generation guided only by the prompt is that we can't always produce exactly the scene, posture or pattern we have in mind. ControlNet partially solves this problem by reinforcing control. For postures, you've certainly seen videos of Greek statues dancing on social media. For patterns, it has been used to create these images with geometric illusions. Some have even described this trend as "Controllism".

But here's the thing, there are a huge number of comments that essentially say these images are uninteresting, they weren't created by humans, there is no artistic intent, so it's not art.

It made me think... On one hand I understand these kinds of reactions but on the other I can't help but think these people wouldn't have had the same speech if they didn't know it was AI-generated.

Just like last year, the judges of the "Colorado State Fair's annual fine art competition" didn't know Jason M. Allen's work "Théâtre d'Opéra Spatial" was created using AI when they awarded it first prize.

In fact, it's impossible on some works to tell the difference between human or AI production.

Also, it's not entirely true that it's not at all created by humans. Behind an image, there is a prompt and you have to iterate a lot before finding the right one, before finding the right parameter settings, etc. It's a process that can take hours or even days. So behind it there is someone giving that famous artistic intent and gradually improving their composition.

Moreover, the AI was trained on a huge number of artworks to learn to generate images, so it makes a synthesis of the production of several people (even if that's a point that can be problematic).

I know many artists and art lovers feel a bit cheated by AI, but I don't think we need to get into some kind of battle. The technology is here now, we have to work with it and learn to use it.

Of course, there are still many problems to be solved regarding creations... but don't AI advances offer an opportunity to rethink our relationship with creation?

item.title: Are LLM Benchmarks Reliable? Not Such a Simple Question...
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Are LLM Benchmarks Reliable? Not Such a Simple Question...

"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure” - Charles Goodhart.

Let's take Hugging Face's Open LLM Leaderboard, very useful for comparing LLMs. It uses 4 benchmarks including the most popular "MMLU".

The MMLU is a set of question-answering to assess "multi-task accuracy" across 57 tasks (math, history, computer science...).

I see 3 points of attention:

1/ The first is that MMLU implementation is not universal. In the LLama 1 scientific paper, the 65B version achieves an MMLU score of 0.637 while at the time, on HuggingFace's leaderboard, it only had 0.488 (before HuggingFace synchronized the leaderboard score with the publication).

So why?

First, it's important to understand an LLM predicts the next word based on its probability.

In the original MMLU implementation, used by the LLama team, the model must, when faced with a question, select an answer among 4 choices (A, B, C or D). The score does not take into account the entire LLM vocabulary, but is limited to these four letters. So even if the expected answer is "B" and the most probable word in the model's vocabulary is "Voyage", followed by "B", the model is deemed correct because consideration is limited to the probabilities of A, B, C or D.

In the HuggingFace Leaderboard implementation that uses the "Harness" variant, we calculate the probabilities the model associates with the full answer sequences, for example "A: This is answer A”, “B: This is answer B", etc. The score is still limited to the 4 given answers but considers the full sequence.

So two MMLU scores from different sources may not be directly comparable depending on implementation.

2/ Some models may have been trained or tuned directly on the benchmarks, causing a data leak from the evaluation set. This is obviously a form of cheating, sometimes intentional. The Hugging Face team normally does what is needed to regularly remove contaminated models from the ranking but some remain. One sign is when "small models" have scores comparable to very large ones. In this case, HuggingFace could request access to the dataset for verification.

3/ Generic metrics like MMLU are probably not relevant for your much more specific use cases (summarizing, interacting with humans etc.)

Benchmarks should be used as a guide and starting point but not absolute truth. Do your own evaluation for your use case and it's very likely the results will surprise you.

item.title: Can Python Really be Replaced Today?
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Can Python Really be Replaced Today?

I often see debates between Python and other programming languages on LinkedIn. Often, the arguments put forward are purely technical arguments from developers (not meant pejoratively).

I would like to very humbly bring here a slightly different perspective to the discussion.

Among the criticisms made against Python, we find the fact that:

  • It is an interpreted and not a compiled language and therefore it is much slower than C or Scala...
  • There is a lack of static data typing, which can lead to confusion and a lack of structure.
  • It has a minimalist design that would offer too much flexibility at the expense of a more rigorous structure.
  • And finally that libraries can become a nightmare to manage.

Yes, all of this is true!

But if we consider what Python has become, no longer from the developer's point of view but at the scale of a company?

From what I observe, the choice of the tech stack and technologies will necessarily influence the way data teams organize themselves and communicate with each other (if they communicate at all :)).

At the same time, I notice that Python is starting to become in companies, more than just a programming language, it is becoming the language of interaction between data teams. Because it is easy to access and versatile and because it has a large community.

If each team has its own language, then I think we create, de facto, silos within the company.

Indeed, if data engineers use Scala and data scientists Python, how could the former do code reviews for the latter? How could a decentralized team structure (Data Mesh) be considered serenely? How to allow anyone to change teams as they wish? How to ensure recruiting developers capable of evolving within the company's technology stack without too much difficulty?

If each team optimizes its tech stack according to its own needs, the result is not necessarily optimal at the global level of the company. It reminds me of "greedy algorithms" (it's my data scientist side) that seek the best choice at each step, but do not always lead to the globally optimal solution.

Despite the promise, every year, of a new language to dethrone Python, I think it is here to stay for a long time.

I know many devs will not agree with me but I think we can certainly have exciting discussions on the subject in the comments!
