item.title: What is a Machine Learning Engineer in this World?
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
What is a Machine Learning Engineer in this World?

It's not a Software Engineer It's not a Data Scientist It's not an MLOps Engineer It's not a Data Engineer It's not a Cloud Engineer / DevOps And yet it's a little bit of all those things at once.

It's being torn between the flexibility needed to prototype and the constraints to impose to smoothly deploy and maintain models.

It's spending the morning pulling your hair out doing Docker in Docker, the afternoon doing transformations on dbt, and the evening to "relax" reading a little scientific publication on the latest advances in LLMs.

It's waking up the next day, looking at your code from the day before and telling yourself it can be simpler, better structured and much better optimized for computing. During the coffee break, learning that what obsesses your colleague ML Engineer himself is learning to optimize CUDA to run a large model on a smartphone.

It's wondering if TensorFlow is still alive or if PyTorch has definitely buried it.

It's having a few strokes of genius, being proud of your CI/CD and a few minutes later miserably failing to cleanly format a yaml file.

It's turning off an EC2/SageMaker instance on AWS when leaving work and on the way home, wondering if it's still on.

It's explaining to your product owner that it's not that simple to prevent an LLM from hallucinating 100% of the time.

It's looking at the code implementation of a library on GitHub rather than its documentation because sometimes it's clearer.

It's spending more time on Udemy or Coursera than in front of your TV.

It's realizing there are no 2 similar profiles of ML Engineers. It's so true that you could be the messiah for some companies and miserably fail the pre-selections for others.

It's seeing your model, once deployed, solve real problems and knowing your work has impact.

It's collaborating with brilliant and interdisciplinary teams.

It's also never stopping learning.

It's realizing you're part of a funny species.

That's what a ML Engineer is like.

item.title: Did Microsoft leak the number of parameters in ChatGPT?
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
A Microsoft publication is causing quite a stir because it appears to have leaked the number of parameters in GPT-3.5 Turbo, which would be 20 billion (20B). This seems rather "small" compared to the very large language models today like Falcon (180B), LLama-2 (70B), etc.

As a reminder, Microsoft is a partner of OpenAI so they certainly have access to this kind of information.

Some think this is a typo and the real number would be closer to 200B, because its bigger brother GPT-3 has 175B parameters.

But when you think about it, there are a number of clues pointing towards the 20B figure:

▶ The GPT-3.5 Turbo API is 10 times cheaper than Text-Davinci-003 (175B). By proportionality, we would arrive at around 20B.
▶ Sam Altman stated last April "I think we're at the end of the era where it's going to be these, like, giant, giant models [...], we'll make them better in other ways."
▶ Models like Mistral (7B) have shown it's possible to do better with fewer parameters.

We already knew, thanks to the famous "Chinchilla" publication, that most LLMs were suboptimal. But if it turns out that GPT-3.5 Turbo really has 20B parameters, it would open up some very interesting possibilities since we can already run 13B LLMs on MacBooks.

How did they do it? We can speculate on elements like knowledge distillation, pruning, longer training times, and above all drastically improving the quality of the training data...

GPT-3.5-Turbo launched in March 2023, so if all of this is confirmed, it would mean OpenAI still has a huge lead over its competitors in terms of know-how.

paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.17680.pdf

item.title: Most embedding models have linguistic bias
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Most embedding models have linguistic bias. Whether for semantic search or LLM-powered QA (which is itself just semantic search with an LLM at the end of the chain), these techniques rely on creating embeddings - high-dimensional vectors capturing semantics. These embeddings, which can be seen as points in a space, are designed to be close together if they come from semantically similar sentences.

However, these models are often linguistically biased. Most models I've tested, whether via Hugging Face's sentence transformers or OpenAI's API, tend to bring texts in the same language closer together, even when more relevant texts exist in other languages.

Concretely, this linguistic bias means that a semantic search engine will tend to prioritize results in the same language as the query formulated by the user. This can be problematic in some cases but overall, it's not necessarily a bad thing. Suppose a user queries the engine with a legal question - since the law depends on the country, it would be relevant for them to get results in the language of their query, which probably corresponds to their country.

Where it gets tricky is when for example the user queries in French to ask for details on English law. Among the relevant documents, the French texts will likely be favored. This is where having an LLM at the end of the chain can compensate for this bias and strengthen the relevance of the response based on the documents but also on its own knowledge.

item.title: Entrepreneurs: having a good idea is not enough to succeed.
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
There is a myth surrounding entrepreneurs that having a good idea is enough to succeed. This seems increasingly true today with the emergence of accessible AI services, especially with Sam Altman's latest announcements (The GPTs). Going from idea to execution appears simpler than ever, but isn't this an illusion?

As I write this, there are likely thousands of people in France who are not from the tech world but have a bright idea to generate cash using a customized chatbot product. However, even brilliant ideas do not magically create applications ready to conquer the CAC 40.

I readily admit that with new generative AI tools, you can prototype faster and do some pretty convincing things very quickly. However, to have a functional, scalable solution is another story.

Without being a multinational, you need some resources and especially a small full-time developer team! Because accompanying this first myth is usually another: believing you can outsource the development of the solution in one go, and that this solution will remain unchanged until the end of time.

An AI-based application, like all applications, requires testing, debugging, and frequent updates. There is both the interface design (the frontend) and the app engine (the backend) to manage. The application will inevitably crash in production at some point, and people will be needed to handle these incidents. And that's without even talking about all the inherent data and ML model challenges. In short, none of this is static.

Yes, AI opens up exciting new perspectives, and I am the first to encourage everyone to take an interest. However, without wanting to dampen anyone's enthusiasm, I invite any determined entrepreneurs to prepare for the challenges associated with software and AI product development.

item.title: Is prompt engineering a scalable long-term approach ?
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
The Scalability Concerns of Relying on Prompt Engineering.

I'm wondering if prompt engineering is a scalable long-term approach. I feel like today a large part of solutions based on LLMs rely on OpenAI/Azure API calls and use more or less complex prompt engineering (chains of prompts, chains of thoughts, routing, etc.).

All these prompts are very sensitive - sometimes a comma changes the output behavior. Prompt templates, like any app feature, need to evolve over time. Some use cases even require periodically adding new ones.

Evolving these prompts inevitably means breaking a precarious balance and going back to a few hours of manual testing. There are still no mature processes for versioning and monitoring prompts and hyperparameters. Simply because there are no very sophisticated methods yet to automatically evaluate text generated by LLMs. This step is still very manual.

Having an open source model with finetuning pipelines seems like a more scalable approach to me (but much more complex and expensive for now). I agree that in terms of cost, relying on APIs is much cheaper for the vast majority of use cases. However, I can't help but think open source is the future.

Curious to hear your thoughts.

item.title: Open source LLMs are sometimes cheaper than APIs
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
There are cases where using an open source LLM is cheaper than going through API calls. The main obstacle to using open source models is the inference cost associated with serving, but you'll see that there are exceptions. I'm extending here Pierre-Carl Langlais' line of thinking. In one of his Linkedin post he describes a text annotation use case via LLMs that is cheaper and faster for him than using APIs.

More generally, I think we need to distinguish between two situations: streaming, where we need to process data in real time, and batch processing, where we can afford to wait.

The chatbot is a good illustration of the streaming case: the user sends their request and expects an immediate response. In this case, going through APIs like OpenAI, Bedrock, Azure or VertexAI is generally more cost effective, because you only pay for what you consume, without having to rent remote machines 24/7 to host the model.

On the other hand, for batch processing, we can afford to wait to build up a large enough data set. We can then rent a machine for the duration of processing and do everything in one go. For example, an A10G GPU (64GB VRAM) on SageMaker only costs $2/hour. We then repeat this routine periodically as needed.

Use cases that lend themselves to batch processing include: text annotation, complex labeling, generating descriptions from summary information, text correction, exam grading, text summarization, annotated dataset generation, document translation, named entity extraction, customer service QA...

And I haven't even talked about all the other advantages, besides cost, that using open source models offers.

item.title: Data Science Careers and Medical Specialties: An Amusing Parallel
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
I found it entertaining to draw a parallel between data science careers and medical specialties, to better convey the diversity of roles. The idea came to me from noticing that many people have difficulty perceiving the nuances (and it’s normal, it’s far from obvious).

▶ Data Science Tech Lead → Medical Director: supervision, strategic decision-making, team management, with a broad understanding of various domains.

▶ Data Scientist (Tabular Data) → Epidemiologist: Analysis of structured data sets, study of models, causes and effects...

▶ Data Scientist (NLP) → Speech Therapist: Understanding and interpretation of human language.

▶ Data Scientist (Computer Vision) → Radiologist: Understanding and interpretation of visual data.

▶ ML Engineer → Biomedical Engineer: Designing industrializable equipment/models.

▶ MLOps Engineer → Hospital Maintenance Engineer: maintenance, monitoring equipment, model lifecycle management.

Obviously these parallels are not 100% relevant. But the idea is that a specialist in one domain is not necessarily competent in all others, even if there is a common foundation of knowledge.

In general, you don't go to a cardiologist for dental problems.

item.title: Riding the LLM Hype Wave
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
I'd be lying if I said there wasn't hype around LLMs. Of course, the emergence of ChatGPT has propelled LLMs into the spotlight. Today, even people outside of data science know what an LLM is or at least know the name and associate it with ChatGPT or similar services.

For my part, having a background in NLP (natural language processing), it was very natural for me to switch to LLMs. And I clearly saw a rupture after ChatGPT.

Hype isn't necessarily a negative phenomenon in itself. It's annoying when it disproportionately focuses attention on something. I don't feel like that's the case here.

Moreover, I notice that this hype has re-energized research, scientific publications, the release of open source packages and frameworks, training... At the same time, many companies are regaining interest in AI. Even the public sector is regaining interest in AI with the recent government initiatives (Artificial Intelligence Generative Committee which includes Yann Le Cun among others).

LLMs and OpenAI are also shaking up the tech giants' hegemony like Google, that doesn't happen every day!

This enthusiasm around AI is also materializing with a multiplication of talks, meetups, conferences. These numerous events offer regular opportunities for exchange and reflection.

Finally, this hype doesn't only benefit Data Scientists or ML Engineers! It benefits the entire Data ecosystem. There are positive externalities for Software Engineers, Data Engineers, Product Owners... and undoubtedly other professions as well. LLMs have also brought all the jobs I just mentioned a little closer together.

This excitement is nice to see and at the same time gives a hard time to all those trying to stay up to date.

We must take advantage of hypes because let's not forget that data science has seen some pretty cold winters. Moreover, amplified by the economic and social conditions of recent years.

So let's enjoy the hype.

item.title: Let's talk about AI agents and LangChain…
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Let's talk about AI agents and LangChain...With LLMs, you need to "code agile". Just as teams need to adapt quickly to changes, these applications must be able to easily absorb technological developments.

Indeed, models, tools, methods and techniques are progressing daily. What is coded today could become obsolete in a few months. Along the way, you may want to change the LLM, vector store, embedding model, etc.

Of course, modularity is already a good practice, we haven't reinvented the wheel. But with the frantic pace of AI, we probably feel this need even more. The idea is to design the most decoupled blocks possible. For example, you can use abstract classes and implement the technical logic in child classes.

Nevertheless, some couplings may remain, for example prompt templates are closely linked to the chosen LLM models. Some technological choices will be more difficult to change. I'm thinking in particular of orchestrators like Langchain, which are central, which are involved in each of the blocks, and which already provide their share of abstractions.

I'll take this opportunity to provide some feedback on Langchain. For classic cases, it does its job, but if you want to do things that are slightly outside the scope, you quickly end up having to reimplement certain components. In general, very simple things become relatively complex to manage.

I ended up recoding a lot of bricks custom. It's more straightforward and easier to debug. The concept of chains is very interesting on paper, but in practice, there are lots of nebulous things and the documentation doesn't explain all the subtleties. Most of the time, I look directly at the code implementation to understand certain behaviors.

LangChain remains a nice utility brick, I use it in particular for the document loader, chunking and conversational memory management.

I haven't tested alternatives to Langchain yet, I'm looking forward to testing LlamaIndex or Haystack.

item.title: The Fleeting Value of LLM Benchmarks
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
You can't improve what you don't measure. However, the relevance of measurement can degrade over time.

Regarding LLMs or machine learning in general, we often rely on benchmarks to rank models...

Yet they have an ephemeral evaluation capability.

They are necessary because they allow, on the one hand, to compare models with each other and, on the other hand, to quantify the progress made when undertaking to improve them.

We can mention the most well-known for LLMs in particular: MMLU HellaSwag, HumanEval...And for embedding models: STS, Glue MS Marco etc.

However, their evaluation power is temporary. At first, they are relevant, but over time, we see a score inflation. New models achieve better results, without necessarily representing a fundamental breakthrough.

You could say that this is a more or less indirect form of overfitting: over time, model designers get to know the benchmark datasets better and better. They consciously or unconsciously adjust the training parameters and datasets to maximize scores.

Some approaches even go so far as to train the models directly on the benchmark datasets, which is obviously cheating. To catch them out, contamination tests can be done but this is not always enough.

Indeed, simple variations of the test data (paraphrases, translations) can easily circumvent these decontamination measures.

It is therefore quite difficult to measure the share of real progress and the share of "overfitting" of the models, solely on benchmark scores.

Ideally, they should be renewed on a regular basis but the work involved would be substantial.

Benchmarks are useful for preselecting models, but nothing beats building evaluation datasets tailored to your specific needs.

item.title: How an Average LLM Can Fool Benchmarks and Match GPT-4
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
How can an average LLM fool benchmarks and achieve performance comparable to GPT-4?

In this scientific article, researchers show how a 13 billion parameter Llama can artificially achieve very high performance, equivalent to GPT-4.

The key lies in contamination: the fact of training the model or adjusting it on data very similar to the test benchmarks, without getting caught. There are contamination tests to mitigate this but they are not infallible.

Current contamination detection methods are based on the search for n-gram overlaps. Simple variations of the test data (paraphrases, translations) can easily circumvent these decontamination measures.

In this study, the researchers propose a more robust decontamination method based on LLMs.

They applied their method to popular datasets, revealing significant previously unknown overlap from the tests. For example, in pretraining sets like RedPajamaData-1T and StarCoderData, they identified an 8 to 18% overlap with HumanEval.

They also found such contamination even in the synthetic datasets generated by GPT-3.5/4, suggesting a potential risk of unintentional contamination.

Link to the article: https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04850

item.title: Questioning the AGI Dream
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
I don't really know what to think about these AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) stories. Many players like OpenAI, Anthropic or Deepmind are pursuing this ancient dream of creating an artificial intelligence surpassing our own.

To achieve AGI, we would first have to define it precisely. But its definition is not really consensus, and a fortiori neither is that of intelligence. On Wikipedia, AGI is defined as follows: "artificial intelligence capable of performing or learning practically any cognitive task characteristic of humans". Does this include the ability to contribute to science? To lead people? To develop the ability to lie? To disobey? Does general intelligence imply some form of autonomy or free will?

One could argue that even without being able to formally define intelligence, this does not prevent recognizing an intelligent person when you come across one. Similarly, it will not prevent researchers from getting closer to AGI without being able to define it. But would we be able to recognize an AGI if we had one in front of us? Would we be humble enough to put a machine on the same pedestal as the human being? That's not sure.

Without completely ruling it out, I am in truth rather skeptical that we will ever achieve it. I am not sure either that the transformer architecture alone allows us to get closer to it. Even by training an LLM on all available knowledge, nothing suggests that we would achieve AGI. We could also increase the LLM size and training time, nevertheless, we are already approaching the limits of what is financially feasible.

Faced with these architectural and economic limits, a new trend is emerging. That of designing systems based on a set of specialized models: MoEs (Mixture of Experts). This approach has gained popularity following rumors that GPT-4 itself is built on this principle.

Even if in the future we realize that AGI is a utopia, it's not that bad. Utopias have been responsible for many advances in the history of science. Moreover, why this desire to pursue AGI? It is not necessary to reach such a level of intelligence to disrupt our societies.

item.title: Speed Learning Machine Learning concepts in 1 Hour
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
If I only had one hour to familiarize myself with an unknown machine learning subject, I would try to choose some steps from the following list (ranked by priority):

  1. Find a short YouTube video explaining the basics of the subject, I usually watch them at 1.5x speed.
  2. Ask ChatGPT for a summary.
  3. Look for a Colab notebook. On Google, the magic trick is to follow your query with the Colab address prefix, for example: “segmentation model site:colab.research.google.com”. The big advantage is that there is no time lost setting up the environment and the explanations are often detailed.
  4. Read experience feedback on Reddit, LinkedIn or Twitter. It is fairly easy, even on LinkedIn, to find relevant posts with the right keywords.
  5. Check if there is a relevant model on Hugging Face. The description pages are often rich in information: usage examples, training methodology, datasets used...
  6. Take a Udemy course, they are often on sale for 10-15€. I think it's fair to pay that amount if it saves me a lot of time. I watch the parts that interest me at 1.5x speed.
  7. Do my own tests and experiments.
  8. Read specialized blog articles (Medium, Towards Data Science...).
  9. Find a GitHub project and analyze the implementation.
  10. Consult scientific publications on the subject.

For purists, it may seem counterintuitive that scientific publications come last. The pragmatic stance here is to emphasize learning by doing. It often allows for faster and more motivating skill building. In a second step, doing usually naturally leads me to read publications, attracted by the curiosity to understand how it works in detail. I also find it simpler to read them after having practiced the subject beforehand.

The other principle is to capitalize on what your peers have already done before you and not to reinvent the wheel.

item.title: 4 Simple Tips for Improving RAG Performance
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Here are four simple tips for improving the performance of your RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation):

  1. Understand the RAG: The RAG combines a "Retrieval" step to find relevant documents for a user query, and a "LLM" step where those documents feed a language model to generate the final response.

  2. You can't improve what you don't measure: Use experiment tracking with tools like MLflow. Log everything necessary to reproduce the experience and analyze it afterwards. This includes scores, prompt templates, queries, retrieved documents, hyperparameters like chunk size, chunk overlap... but also matplotlib visualizations etc. This will avoid the "It was better before but I don't know what I changed". There are still a lot of projects navigating by sight.

  3. Evaluation of response quality: How to evaluate LLM responses? What metrics? This is still a complex area, and for good reason it is an active subject of research. Simple metrics like ROUGE can be used but they are limited because they are based solely on the number of common n-grams between the LLM prediction and the target. There is also BertScore to consider, or using another LLM to evaluate the final response. It's up to you to choose your method.

  4. Evaluation of Retrieval: What we can do much more easily, however, is measure the ability of retrieval to find relevant documents. Prepare an evaluation dataset with queries and expected relevant documents. The idea is then to compare the documents retrieved by the retrieval to the relevant documents. The metrics to use here are similar to those of recommendation systems: Hitrate, Precision@k, Recall@k, MAP.

  5. Query optimization: The assumption of retrieval is the semantic similarity between documents to be retrieved and the user query. This is a very strong assumption that is often inaccurate. To improve this, explore strategies such as query transformation. You can use reformulation via an LLM or go through more classic NLP techniques like NER for keyword extraction, it's up to you. Also consider specialized embedders that have been specifically trained on question-answer pairs. Also pay attention to some embedders that have a fairly low token limit (128 tokens for some Hugging Face models).

item.title: From Classic ML to LLMs: Similar Development Trajectories?
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
It's interesting to see how certain patterns in Machine Learning seem to recur, including with LLMs:

Classic ML:

  • Step 1: The nature of the model matters.
  • Step 2: The quantity of data matters.
  • Step 3: Feature engineering matters, you have to find the magic feature.
  • Step 4: The quality of the data matters.
  • Step 5: No point trying to get an exceptional model, it's more interesting to have an ensemble of average models.

LLMs:

  • Step 1: The number of parameters matters.
  • Step 2: The quantity of data matters.
  • Step 3: The length of the context window matters.
  • Step 4: The quality of the data matters.
  • Step 5: No point trying to get an exceptional model, it's more interesting to have an ensemble of specialized models (Mixture of Experts).

Are we rediscovering the same best practices viewed from a different angle every time? Or is this rather a natural evolution of priorities as ML models develop? That is, first emphasize the model itself, then the quality of the data, and finally ensemble approaches.

In any case, two principles seem universal:

The first: "Garbage doesn't turn into gold, no matter how much math you throw at it" (I believe that's a quote from Cassie Kozyrkov).

The second: united we stand. With tabular data, the star algorithms come from ensemble methods: XGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest, etc. LLMs seem to be following the same trajectory.

item.title: The Decline of TensorFlow, The Rise of PyTorch
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
TensorFlow was once essential, but I see fewer and fewer reasons to use it today. PyTorch seems to be establishing itself as the go-to deep learning framework.

TensorFlow from Google or PyTorch from Meta?

I was originally very partial to TensorFlow because it had a large community and was very popular. Moreover, Andrew Ng's essential deep learning course used this framework.

I was actually surprised to see him offer a generative AI course last year with AWS and Hugging Face - a direct competitor of Google and a major player in the PyTorch ecosystem. Andrew Ng no longer works for Google, but I still see this as a form of repudiation.

The fact is, the torch has set the flow on fire. The trend has reversed and the demand for PyTorch has surpassed that of TensorFlow on Stack Overflow.

PyTorch has several decisive advantages:

▶ Developed specifically for Python, it is more intuitive and "Pythonic", simpler to debug. While TensorFlow is more complex, with a higher barrier to entry.

▶ Its ease of use accelerated its adoption in research, followed by students and now industry.

▶ Hugging Face has greatly contributed to the craze around PyTorch. Today, nearly 90% of models in the hub are exclusive to PyTorch. Moreover, to my knowledge, there are no LLMs developed in TensorFlow.

The curve shows an acceleration of the decline starting in 2020, the year when:

  • Google DeepMind announced switching from TensorFlow to JAX, Google's new framework, to accelerate its development.
  • OpenAI standardized the use of PyTorch within its organization.
  • PyTorch facilitated large-scale model deployment via TorchServe, its equivalent of TensorFlow Serving.

And finally, the cornerstone of TensorFlow, which was Keras, can now be used with PyTorch.

Do you still see reasons to use TensorFlow?

item.title: Math Skills vs. Pragmatism in Data Science
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Math skills are often considered fundamental to becoming a data scientist. This is true, but we often forget to mention that in practice, machine learning is above all a pragmatic discipline.

It's important to stress this because theory and practice sometimes pursue distinct objectives, and some students who love math could be disappointed by this on-the-ground reality.

This pragmatism means that we don't judge an idea by whether it's beautiful or neatly constructed, but by its practical consequences. In other words, whether it yields good results, which can be frustrating at times.

Even though math is fundamental, data science in practice is not the pursuit of pure truth.

It's not the admiration of an elegant formula that solves everything. It's not about finding the right way to converge towards the global minimum (if that's even possible). Large language models themselves are the result of an idea that seems very simple a priori: predict the next word based on the previous ones. There is no explicit mechanism that would allow it to reason. But implemented on a massive scale of data, it produces impressive results. If this approach has become widespread, it's not because it was the most elegant idea, but because it's the one that works best, for now.

The data scientist must be prepared:

  • To examine the data in detail, even if it's laborious
  • To be able to abandon appealing but ineffective ideas
  • To explore avenues, however simple or counterintuitive they may seem at first
  • To sometimes focus more on engineering at the expense of the scientific aspect

I'm not minimizing the value of mathematical theory in the least - it remains essential. I'm simply offering a more nuanced perspective. Because in data science, the value created is measured above all by the ability to solve client problems or create opportunities.

If we can combine efficiency and elegance, so much the better. If not, we'll keep just the efficiency.

item.title: The Non-Determinism of OpenAI and Anthropic Models
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI and Anthropic's models are not deterministic, even at temperature zero and with a fixed seed, and this can be a real problem.

How is it that some models are not deterministic under these conditions? This is a question I've been asking myself for some time now.

In manipulating models, I observed that with a fixed prompt and temperature at zero, the output was not always the same. At the time, I thought it was a bug, a rounding issue, or that there was deliberately some residual randomness for some unknown reason. I didn't really investigate the issue thoroughly.

But in some cases, it's quite essential to guarantee reproducible results, for example in a testing/experimentation tracking phase.

Temperature is the parameter that controls a dose of randomness and therefore the model's dose of creativity.

This "T" comes into play in the model's final layer, the softmax, to transform the output values into a probability distribution. When T tends towards 0, it acts as an amplifier and the highest probability tends towards 1, all others towards 0. In other words, this amounts to always selecting the most probable word (like an argmax).

Conversely, when T tends towards 1, it reduces differences between probabilities and the distribution becomes more uniform, thus giving the model the opportunity to vary its choice of words.

OpenAI and Anthropic's models, even with a temperature of 0, are not deterministic. What? A result that changes 1 out of 5 times can't be a rounding problem. It also can't be a bug shared by 2 different services.

Anthropic and OpenAI only provide vague answers on this subject.

Some have hypothesized that since GPT-4 would be a Mixture of Experts, it would have to choose an expert for each token, and this choice would depend on its availability. In other words, if it's already busy processing other requests, another expert takes over, thus causing a difference.

GPT-3.5 Turbo also isn't deterministic, so according to the preceding hypothesis it too would be a Mixture of Experts.

What is also interesting is that Mixtral models seem to be deterministic, even though they too are Mixtures of Experts...

So, MoE? Floating point operations? Designers' choice?

item.title: Assessing the Criticality of AI Failures
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
What is the criticality of a bad prediction from your algorithm? In my opinion this is one of the first questions to ask before considering a generative AI or AI project in general.

It's encouraging to see public knowledge about AI progressing. However, I think some aspects still require awareness-building, like choosing and framing use cases.

With the emergence of generative AI services (ChatGPT, MidJourney, etc.) and their democratization, business ideas are blossoming. I sometimes hear project ideas or startup ideas around me that make me wince because they don't take into account cases that could go wrong.

Machine learning solutions come from statistical methods, so a prediction will never be 100% reliable. What’s worse, in some cases they’re not even deterministic – they can vary from one run to another. We have to work with that and therefore choose use cases accordingly.

With that in mind, a question that naturally arises is: when the algorithm is wrong, what will the consequences be?

For a programming assistant solution like Github Copilot, criticality is almost zero. If the code suggestion is bad, it’s not serious, you’re there to correct it, there’s a human in the loop.

For an autonomous vehicle solution, a failure can be very critical – in the worst case, it can take a life.

In any case, whatever the project, I think it's always healthy to think about cases that can go wrong and their consequences. What happens if my solution discriminates against users? If it misinforms because of hallucinations? If it generates offensive content? Dangerous content? If it gives access to sensitive information? If it causes users to lose money?

All this to say that if the slightest prediction error is critical for your business, AI is probably not the right path.

In my opinion, the "good" use cases are those that tolerate a certain error rate and for which failures do not have serious consequences. In particular, use cases with a "human in the loop" are generally relatively safe.

item.title: RAG vs Finetuning - Complementary not Opposing
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
RAG and finetuning are often opposed: Should we fine-tune our LLM or do RAG? In reality, the approaches do not oppose each other. On the contrary, they complement each other.

RAG, which needs no introduction, allows querying an external knowledge base to enrich the context provided to the LLM. We thus add the relevant documents to the prompt. This approach is very interesting when dealing with evolving information because we update the database, not the model, which is much simpler and less expensive. The double advantage is that by constraining the model to rely on documents, we reduce its propensity to hallucinate.

The downside is that by adding both context, instructions, documents, thought processes (Chain of Thought), and finally few-shot examples to the prompt, the prompt becomes a whole little booklet.

Even though LLMs have increasingly impressive ingestion capacities (context window of 200k tokens for Claude 2 and 128k for GPT-4), they are designed such that they have attention loss when they have to "read novels". In particular, their focus is on the beginning and the end, with potentially lost information in the middle, hence the interest in staying concise (see the paper "Lost in the Middle").

Finetuning, on the other hand, allows adjusting the LLM by training it on your own dataset. This allows it to learn things specific to your field, jargon, tone, behavior, but also to align it with your values... This not only improves its relevance but also means that if you use RAG on top, there will be even less to make explicit in the prompt, thus giving the LLM the opportunity to focus on the key information.

A recent scientific publication has moreover quantified the performance gain of the finetuning + RAG method. (RAG vs Finetuning)

When possible, the best approach is to do both.

item.title: Navigating the Jungle of LLM Quantization Formats, GGUF, GPTQ, AWQ and EXL2 - Which One To Pick?
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Quantizing LLMs reduces calculation precision and thus the required GPU resources, but it can sometimes be a real jungle trying to find your way among all the existing formats.

GGUF, GPTQ, AWQ, EXL2... Which quantization format to choose and why?

There are so many standards and tools because quantization is not just about rounding values. There are in fact more advanced strategies and different philosophies. It's a bit like images with JPEG, PNG, SVG, WEBP formats...

Take GGUF, the format popularized by llama.cpp, its goal is to reduce precision while optimizing calculations from a CPU perspective, with a particular focus on Apple hardware. It remains possible to offload some of the weights to the GPU for more speed. To run an LLM locally, it's therefore a good candidate, especially if you have a Mac.

GPTQ is oriented towards GPU inference performance. It quantizes the weights by minimizing error thanks to a calibration dataset. This allows comparing the outputs of the full precision and quantized model. At inference, GPTQ dynamically "dequantizes" the weights in float16 to limit loss of precision, all with low impact on GPU memory.

AWQ is based on the observation that ~1% of weights contribute significantly to model performance; these must therefore be treated with special care by applying per-channel scaling. AWQ uses a dataset to analyze activation distributions during inference and identify critical weights. AWQ is faster at inference than GPTQ and also seems to have better perplexity but requires slightly more VRAM.

EXL2 uses the GPTQ philosophy but allows mixing weight precisions within the same model. Some critical weights thus retain high precision, with the rest being more quantized to optimize performance. EXL2 probably offers the fastest inference, at the cost of slightly higher VRAM consumption than AWQ.

To finetune a quantized LLM with QLoRA, you’ll only be able to do it with GPTQ (or with bitsandbytes for on-the-fly quantization).

If you want to avoid quantizing an LLM yourself, the user TheBloke on Huggingface has close to 4000 models ready to use in GPTQ, GGUF or AWQ formats.

But things are moving so fast, it’s hard to stay abreast of the latest advances and it wouldn't be surprising to see new standards emerge in the coming months.

item.title: Padding strategy matters when Fine tuning LLMs
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
A poor padding strategy can disrupt an LLM after fine-tuning, and the reasons are quite subtle. This is especially true since there is no pad_token in the Llama2 or Mistral tokenizers.

A neural network is a sequence of matrix multiplications. When working with text and variable sequence lengths, padding is required to normalize them to a common length to allow matrix representation.

This padding simply consists of filling the sequences with a special token until they reach the length of the longest sequence in the batch.

It turns out that most LLMs were pre-trained without padding. As decoders, they predict the next word based on previous words. It is then enough to split the training corpus into equal sequence lengths and train the model on it (even if sometimes the splitting is not very graceful). No need for padding, besides in many models like Mistral or Llama2, the padding token doesn't even exist in the tokenizer.

When fine-tuning these models on specific instructions, we provide the instructions and expected responses in a single block (we concatenate both). There is no reason for the sequences to be the same length. To process all of this in batches, padding is then required. Having no padding token, one way to get by is to use the eos (end of sequence) or unk (unknown) token instead.

Then, what do we do? Right or left padding?

  • With eos, I'm personally not very comfortable doing left padding: the model is asked to stop the sequence even though it hasn't started. Doing right padding, why not.
  • With <unk>, doing left or right padding should be fairly equivalent.

On the other hand for inference, you have in my opinion no choice but to do left padding. Simply because the decoder will rely on your last token to predict the next one; if it's padding, the quality of the response will be altered.

One last approach that seems quite elegant and effective for fine-tuning is to do as in initial training: no padding, concatenate the entire question-answer dataset and slice it into identical chunks of N tokens.

Curious to know your padding strategies.

item.title: Why bigger context windows won't make RAG disappear.
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
We sometimes hear that RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) is destined to disappear because LLMs have an increasingly large context window and can therefore receive more and more words.

In other words, we'll soon be able to pass an entire database to the LLM in one prompt and let it figure it out to answer the question asked.

Personally, I don't think this is a good approach, and for several reasons:

The computational cost increases quadratically with the number of words. More simply put, the more words you send to an LLM, the more you tax the GPU memory.

If you host the LLM yourself on a GPU instance, the direct consequence is that you'll probably have to opt for a larger instance, so pay more.

If you go through an API, the consequence is also that it's more expensive because you pay per token. You'll also hit query rate limits faster.

With very long prompts, context loss or hallucinations are encouraged (see the "Lost in the Middle" publication).

And finally, I haven't been able to experiment with such solutions with better results than RAG.

From my point of view, it's more expensive, it takes longer, and it's generally not as good.

All of this reminds me a bit of deep learning a few years ago. The approach was to realize that we have mind-boggling data streams and extraordinary computing capabilities, so we might as well use them. Even if the data is not quality, the promise was that quantity would make up for it.

We’ve come back a bit from that narrative today by saying that we don't need that much data; it must, however, be qualitative.

item.title: Is There a Future for On-Device Open Source LLMs?
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
One obstacle to using open source LLMs is the cost of hosting them on GPU instances in the cloud. But perhaps there is a future for on-device open source?

From what I've seen, the overwhelming majority of AI products using LLMs are based on API calls to services like OpenAI, Bedrock or Vertex AI. And that makes sense - it's quick to set up, cheaper to run, and there's no heavy infrastructure to manage.

In a previous post I made a distinction between use cases requiring an instant response (streaming) like chatbots, and those that can be handled in batches like annotation, proofreading, etc. In the latter case, you just rent a GPU instance in the cloud for the duration of the task, not 24/7. It's an inexpensive way to benefit from open source LLMs.

I imagine that in the future, a new trend may emerge for open source models - on-device. For example, for a corporate chatbot, instead of designing cloud infrastructure and a web UI for employees, the work would consist of directly (or partially) downloadable applications that run from laptops (also bringing technical and practical challenges).

When you think about it, LLMs are increasingly optimized and the chips embedded in computers more and more powerful. There are also massive investments happening in the space right now.

Obviously with all this, Apple MacBooks with their M-series chips are ahead and seem like natural candidates to run LLMs locally, even if AMD and Intel are working hard playing catch up.

I wonder if for some time now Apple has been secretly conceiving its own on-device LLM that will interact with the entire macOS ecosystem.

item.title: Managing a Mainstream Open Source Library is Tough
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Managing a mainstream open-source library is a full-time job that requires implementing an efficient workflow to avoid being overwhelmed.

This is particularly noticeable with Langchain, where at certain times of the day, you refresh the Pull Requests page on GitHub, and there's almost a new one every 10 minutes.

While I'm not a fan of all Langchain's features, I'm quite admiring of the daily workload of the dev teams: nearly 10,000 Pull Requests processed to date for ~2,400 contributors. To handle this flow of code to review, they have implemented the following workflow:

To contribute, you must follow the standard "fork and pull request" procedure, meaning you cannot push directly to their repo; you must make a PR from a fork you have modified.

Before coding anything, you must install the project and its various dependencies with poetry, which will also create a virtual environment for you and centralize all project configurations in the pyproject.toml file.

If you implement a new feature, you will need to document it, add unit tests (and integration tests if necessary), and provide a Jupyter notebook to facilitate understanding and provide concrete usage examples.

Then your code will have to pass a battery of tests, including the following technologies:

  • pytest for unit tests / integration tests.
  • ruff, a super-fast linter / code formatter written in Rust.
  • mypy, which will ensure that all the typing of your functions is consistent.
  • codespell will search for any typos that may have crept into your comments / docstrings.

(Incidentally, it's interesting to see that they don't use GitHub pre-commit).

Makefile is used to automate the commands to be executed, so you can run "make test", "make format", "make lint", etc., locally to check your code.

Finally, when you push your PR, a GitHub Actions CI will trigger to perform the same checks as mentioned above, but additionally, it will ensure code compatibility with Python versions 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, and 3.11.

If your proposal passes all tests and is deemed worthy of interest, it will be reviewed by a team member and potentially merged.

This will undoubtedly put off more than one person, but the idea is to guarantee and maintain a high level of quality. This approach will allow filtering, simplify the review, and decrease the time spent on it.

There are undoubtedly some good practices to be gained.

item.title: The Role of Language in Reasoning and Conceptualization
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Yann LeCun's recent statements about language not being necessary for reasoning are as fascinating as they are divisive. Among other things, he emphasizes that animals or children acquire basic knowledge through their senses. He adds that sight allows for collecting a wealth of information much faster than one could by reading a book. Language would ultimately be the cherry on top, but one would first need to build the cake.

However, even if we read fewer words per second than we see images, language seems to be very efficient in compressing concepts into relatively few symbols. Something that struck me when I started getting interested in Stable Diffusion and Imagen, the famous models that generate images in response to a prompt, is that language plays a predominant role.

Indeed, these models are composed of two sub-models: the first encodes the text of the prompt into embeddings, which are then passed to the second diffusion model (UNet) to generate an image. In Google's publication on Imagen, one can read that the researchers found, quite surprisingly, that increasing the number of parameters in the text encoder contributed much more to improving the quality of the generated image than increasing the number of parameters in the UNet.

From this empirical observation, one is tempted to say that even if language is not a priori necessary for reasoning, it still seems to simplify many things in the process of creation and conceptualization.

The boundaries between AI, philosophy, and neuroscience are sometimes thin, and these fields intersect and influence each other in fascinating ways.

item.title: Google's Python Style Guide for Data Scientists
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
Most Data Scientists have learned to code well on the job. Indeed, higher education generally focuses more on theory (mathematics, statistics, etc.) rather than software engineering, deployment, etc.

I don't know if it's a good or bad choice, the attraction to theory is probably also a bit cultural, and it's also what has produced some exceptional profiles that shine internationally along the way.

In any case, for the rest, the mere mortals who have to improve the quality of their code on a daily basis, Google has made available their best practices and their development style in Python (apparently, it's also a subject for them). We're talking about style because it's primarily a matter of preferences, and also because Python has its own usages and "tacit conventions", we're talking about coding in a "Pythonic" way.

This is a useful document for anyone who wants to improve in this area, especially since the choices are argued. This is important because sometimes certain recommendations or "Craftsman" rules can seem a bit sectarian :)

Link to the document:
https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html

item.title: RAG with LLMs: Easy to POC, Hard to Iterate On.
item.dc:creator: aniszakari
item.content:encoded:
The paradox of LLMs is that they have made POCs (Proofs of Concept) incredibly easy to create, but at the same time, they have made iterating on the product more difficult. This is particularly visible with RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) systems.

RAG systems are initially very simple systems; they require relatively little effort to build with frameworks/libraries like LangChain or LlamaIndex. This generic approach generally works very well on a limited test subset.

Then, over time, we must inevitably complexify the solution to improve its performance and create custom code blocks for the use case, while keeping production constraints in mind. We often find ourselves simultaneously optimizing 5 opposing axes:

1) The relevance of the system's response (effectively provides the expected answer).
2) The behavior of the LLM (tone, output format in JSON/XML, etc.).
3) The system's latency (time between the message and the response).
4) The cost of a system response.
5) The complexity of the solution.

Optimize the relevance of the response and, with the sensitivity of prompts and the system, you end up altering the behavior of the LLM.

Separate the optimization step for relevance and behavior into two distinct independent phases so that one does not influence the other, and you now end up with higher latency and cost.

Use a smaller and faster LLM, you improve latency but increase the complexity of the solution by having to incorporate more context and examples into the prompts.

The "one size fits all approach" works very well and very quickly at the POC stage. To take it a step further, more creativity, more customization, and more thought about the data and overall system design will be required.
